Welcome:
T
hose Who Wander is a dynamic 
game system distinct for its 
branching character paths, diverse 
and versatile parentages, enigmatic 
and awakening heirlooms, 
mechanically defining character 
backgrounds, and more.
The game’s name comes from the popular line, “Not 
all those who wander are lost,” originally penned by 
J.R.R. Tolkien. In more ways than one, Those Who 
Wander epitomizes the journey made of numberless 
steps. Each step is a decision—left or right. And each 
decision leaves its mark on you. No matter where you 
wander, we hope you feel at home all along the way.
Your story really begins before you were born. In 
Those Who Wander, you choose two birth parents from 
whom you inherit your innate and physiological traits. 
Will you choose two human parents, an elven father 
and an orc mother? Or any one of hundreds of other 
unique pairings? The choice is yours.
Biology is not destiny. The people and culture that 
raised you and the choices you made while growing up 
are what developed and molded you. Your background 
supplies all your learned traits, including abilities, 
proficiencies, language, training, and more. Are you 
an artist or a warrior? A miner or a mathematician?
Like heroes before you, you inherited or discovered 
an object of strange powers. After some time, this 
heirloom awakens, sharing its secrets and hidden 
powers with you as you develop your own.
Armed with your parentage, background, and 
heirloom, you embark on your heroic campaign. The 
greatest journey begins with a single step. Do you 
choose left or right? Your character progresses over the 
course of the campaign using the new step system. At 
each juncture, you choose between no more than two 
character features. But the options multiply almost 
exponentially. Over time, you and your fellow party 
members grow ever more diverse and specialized in 
your powers.
No matter who you are as a player, you can find 
yourself mirrored in Those Who Wander, with options 
for prosthetics and wheelchairs, any parentage pairing, 
original creature and peoples lore, and viable blind 
and deaf heroes. What’s more, player agency is nigh 
inviolable.
Not only is player choice held in high regard, care 
has been taken to place players in the spotlight and 
keep them there with combat mechanics that keep the 
players’ dice rolling and allow the storytellers to do 
what they do best.
Those Who Wander is backward-compatible with the 
fifth edition of the world’s most-played roleplaying 
game. That means you can run a 5e adventure with 
virtually no conversion necessary. If you are familiar 
with 5e, the mechanics presented here will feel 
familiar, but with countless novel applications.
We hope this game, and the worlds it creates for 
you and your party, feel like your own. Embark, 
adventurers! This journey is wholly yours.

Chapter 1: Getting Started
W
hat constitutes a player character? 
Is it who their parents were, what 
they’ve done until now, what 
they carry with them, or the 
skills that nature and training 
gave them? Yes, it’s partly all of 
that. But there are indefinable 
qualities that make up a character as well, things you 
won’t find in any book: it’s you, the player, the one 
holding the character sheet, who breathes life and 
personality into what otherwise would only be paper 
and numbers.
In Those Who Wander, you build a character out of 
five main building blocks: parentage, background, 
heirloom, abilities, and the first step of your 
adventuring career. Using these defining elements 
and your own imagination, you bring your character 
to life.
Physical Disability:
Those Who Wander makes no assumptions about 
whether your character is able-bodied or disabled. 
Should you choose to create a character who is 
disabled, options are provided for Blind and Deaf 
characters, as well as prosthetic limbs and wheelchairs.
Characters who use mobility aids or other assistive 
devices are assumed to have them included among 
their starting equipment and are assumed to be a part 
of the character, so any attacks targeting your aid or 
device is considered an attack against you instead.
At the player’s and storyteller’s discretion, a 
character with only one gripping hand and no upper 
prosthesis cannot wield two-handed weapons and 
ignores the versatile weapon property. 
Blindness is a spectrum. Blind characters have either 
varying degrees of vision or no sight at all. A Blind 
character has the following traits:
•	 Choose a number between −1 and −5 (−1 being 
Blindness that interferes with reading and cooking 
to −5 being a complete lack of sight). Apply this 
number to attack checks and ability checks that rely 
on sight.
•	 Reduce the range of your ranged spell attacks to 
5 feet, unless an ally is taking the Help action to 
guide your aim.
•	 Your primary sense is hearing (while all nonblind 
characters’ primary sense is sight) and you’re 
described as a hearing creature.
•	 You’re immune to visual effects that cause the 
disoriented condition.
Deafness is a spectrum. Deaf characters have either 
varying degrees of hearing or hear nothing at all. A 
Deaf character has the following traits:
•	 Choose a number between −1 and −5 (−1 being 
Deafness that interferes with communicating 
verbally to −5 being a complete lack of hearing). 
Apply this number to ability checks that rely on 
hearing.
•	 You have resistance to thunder damage and 
immunity to audible effects that cause the 
disoriented condition.
•	 A Deaf character is unaffected by the silence spell 
unless they attempt to speak vocally. They can 
provide their articulated spell component by 
using the sign languages they’re fluent in or visual 
vernacular.

Abilities:
Every creature has six abilities (Strength, Agility, 
Health, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Presence). For 
more information on abilities and how they’re used in 
play, see the “Playing the Game” chapter.
First Step:
“Right or left. It’s a simple decision, seemingly 
insignificant at the time. But a series of lefts or rights 
leads to vastly different destinations.”
Any character’s first step is a simple decision: A or B, 
left or right, preternatural or scrappy. And each step 
on the path of character progression is just as simple, 
with no more than two options each time. Obviously, 
these simple choices over time have consequences, 
and the characters become increasingly diverse in 
specialization and party role over time. But each time 
it’s still a choice between just two options.
This binary choice makes the game simple enough 
for even the newest of players to grasp: one step at 
a time, even while making progression an integral 
part of discovering who a character is. It’s most 
satisfying when character progression reflects character 
development.
But for now, all you have to do is choose between 
two options and record the accompanying feature and 
Health Die on your character sheet.

Come Together:
Don’t go it alone. Your character can team up with 
other players’ characters to form an adventuring party. 
Make sure that the group’s goals and values have 
enough overlap to keep the party together.
Worldbuilding:
The first time you sit down with your fellow players, 
you should together come up with a campaign premise 
everyone at the table is happy with. Coming up with 
a campaign can be a collaborative activity that often 
starts with the storyteller, though anyone can take 
initiative on this.
Some start like J.R.R. Tolkien, who created a 
fictional language or two first and then began writing 
creation myths and detailed histories of his fantasy 
setting. That’s known as the top-down approach. The 
approach starts with the big picture and then works 
its way down. That approach can be overwhelming to 
new storytellers, so another option is to go bottom-
Rosa wants Holly to be a mysterious and insightful spellcaster, 
so they make her highest ability Presence, followed by Wisdom. 
Holly is also nimble and hardy, so her Agility and Health abilities 
are the next highest abilities. They round out Holly’s abilities 
with Intelligence next and Strength as the lowest.
Holly’s abilities look like this: Strength −1, Agility +1, Health +1, 
Intelligence +0, Wisdom +2, Presence +2.
Rosa wants Holly to become a powerful spellcaster. The Orb of 
the Seer was a good choice for this theme, and Rosa augments 
it by choosing preternatural as Holly’s first step. They record 
Holly’s cantrips and spells on their character sheet and choose 
Presence as her spellcasting ability.
Holly has a starting wealth score of 1, meaning she can obtain 
as many items with a value score of 0 as she wants and a single 
item with a value score of 1. She purchases darts, with a value 
score of 0, without lowering her wealth score. But purchasing 
a spear, with a value score of 1, lowers her wealth score by 0, 
leaving her broke.

We recommend a third option: the given-new 
method.
Given-New Method:
The basic idea of the given-new method is that, before 
introducing new information, it’s best to bring to 
mind what people have heard before. This is what 
fleshes out the campaign world without having to be 
detailed.
Most players already have a mental library of 
fantasy and sci-fi tropes. They've watched The Lord of 
the Rings or Star Wars, read Earthsea or Ender’s Game, 
or collected comic books or manga. When you say, 
“Let’s play an epic fantasy game,” they already have an 
idea of what that might involve.
It might be tempting, when building a new 
campaign setting, to throw something completely new 
at your fellow players. But a totally unfamiliar world is 
disorienting for players and a lot of unnecessary work 
for storytellers who have to build literally everything 
from scratch.
Still, you wouldn’t be building a new campaign 
setting if middle-age Earth worked just fine. You want 
to create something different, something new.
If you want your fellow players to hit the ground 
running while still flexing your creative muscles, give 
them a mix of the familiar (the given) and your own 
spin (the new). The general rule is one given and at 
least two news. For example, you can say you want 
a medieval fantasy setting, but the beasts of burden, 
pets, and mounts are all dinosaurs and a pantheon of 
gods personally rule separate city-states.
Before or during that first meeting, write down 
what your campaign setting is most like and two or 
three important ways it’s original. This is your pitch.
The Pitch:
Unless you’re planning on live-streaming your 
campaign setting, you have one very specific audience 
in mind: your fellow players. Once you’ve written 
your pitch, it’s time to throw it to them.
It’s like you’re a writer pitching to a 
publisher. If your fellow players don’t 
like your pitch, go back to the drawing 
board or pitch it to a different group. 
Eventually, you’ll find a pitch your group 
likes or a group who likes your pitch. When you’ve 
found a match, you can begin the next step.
The Spotlight:
Unlike fantasy authors, you don’t create every 
character in the story. Each of the players plays one 
hero. The storyteller is everything else.
Before going further, storytellers should ask each 
player what character they want to play in your 
setting. Upon hearing the pitch, many players already 
have a rough idea of who they want to play. A good 
pitch usually sets their imaginations loose. Storytellers 
should find out everything they can about who the 
players want to play. Their answers are the story seeds 
the storytellers can use to worldbuild.
For example, if a player says, “I want to play the 
brash, illegitimate daughter of the king,” you need to 
create a kingdom and a king.
“I want to play a detective with amnesia about the 
last few weeks.” You need to create a compelling story 
about what transpired during that bout of amnesia.
“I want to be a priest devoted to the god of love.” 
If there’s no god of love in your setting, make one. Or 
have the player do it.
Make sure there is room in the world for the kinds 
of characters the players want to play. If the pitch 
is that there are talking dinosaurs in your setting, a 
player might really gravitate toward that idea. That

Safety Tools:
We strongly encourage using safety tools to make the 
game a fun and rewarding experience for everyone at 
the table. Generally, foster a culture of communication 
and trust at your table. This starts with valuing the 
enjoyment and well-being of others as much as you 
value your own. And be ready and willing to change 
aspects of the campaign that really aren’t working for 
one or more people at your table.
Be sure that when establishing safety tools you do 
not press for details by asking or even wondering 
aloud why, for example, a player has arachnophobia. 
No one owes you their trauma.
Film Analogy
One safety tool is to treat the game a bit like a movie 
player. Do this by, first of all, establishing a content 
rating you can all agree on. Just as movies have ratings 
(Adult, Teen, Kids, etc.), so too can your game. 
You can even establish levels for different kinds of 
content. For example, maybe your group is okay with 
adult-level violence, but the sexual content is set to 
just teen-level. Or vice versa. Make sure everyone is 
comfortable with the rating. Setting a content rating 
frees the storyteller and players to push the game in 
any pre-approved direction confident that everyone is 
on board and it’s not crossing any line.
Of course, not everything can be anticipated before 
the game begins. Accordingly, the movie analogy can 
come into play mid-session as well. Give fellow players 
the ability to Rewind, Pause, Resume, or Fast Forward 
the game. During a session, storytellers or players can 
say these commands aloud or tap a prepared card.
Rewind (<<). The rewind command is used when 
a player or storyteller doesn’t like the way something 
went and wants to go back and play it over again or 
adjust it. This shouldn’t be used to merely reroll dice, 
but any other reason is fine.
Pause (II). The pause command is used when a 
player or storyteller wants to continue playing but 
needs a break before doing so.
Continue (>). The continue command is used when 
a break is ending and the player is ready to resume the 
game session.
Fast Forward (>>). The fast forward command is 
used when a player or storyteller wants to skip to the 
next scene, either because something has come up 
that is uncomfortable in this scene or to control the 
pacing.
Finally, after the game session is over, take some 
time to talk about what everyone liked and what could 
have gone better. Adjust content ratings and other 
safety tools, as needed. As before, there should be no 
pressure to divulge why a player or storyteller wants a 
change.
The film analogy is just one suite of safety tools. 
Feel free to use any other that works for everyone 
at your table. By using safety tools, you respect the 
people at your table and foster an environment where 
everyone can consistently have fun.
Final Word:
We creators never endorse or condone hazardous 
behavior, gaslighting, or psychological or emotional 
manipulation. If you, or someone else, are affected

Complex Parentage:
With the rules provided above, you can create a 
character of up to two parentages, such as a character 
with both elven and orc parentage. But should an elf-
orc have a child with a dwarf-gnome, what parentage 
traits does their offspring have?
With storyteller permission, you can create 
characters of more than two parentages using the 
following point-buy system. Choose traits from the 
Parentage Traits table until you have a total somewhere 
between 11 and 17, with the most balanced characters 
having a number between 13 and 16. Using this 
method, you can create a balanced character with any 
number of parentages in their ancestry.

Miner:
In order to mine, you need a Strength of +0 or higher. 
Consult the Metalworking and Gemcutting sections 
of Crafting for the time it takes to mine various ores 
and gems.
Finding a Mine. Finding a mine that is nearby 
and also available for public use can be difficult. Not 
every settlement is going to have a nearby mine and 
those that do are often owned by people who don’t 
allow anyone other than those they employ to use it. 
Some owners allow outsiders to use their mine for an 
hourly fee. 
Mining Ore and Gems. Depending on the mine, 
you’re either mining ore directly with the chance 
of finding a gem or you’re mining a gemstone vein 
directly, and in that case, you only receive the 
corresponding gemstone. 
Selling Ore and Gems. If the mine that you’re 
using is owed by someone, they typically buy what 
you’ve mined. Their purchasing prices are a lot stricter 
than if you went to a shop and sold it or found an 
individual buyer.

Attunement:
Some magic items require a creature to form a bond 
with them before their magical properties can be used. 
This bond is called attunement, and all heirlooms 
and certain items have a prerequisite for it. If the 
prerequisite is to be a spellcaster, a creature qualifies if 
it can cast at least one spell using its traits or features, 
not using a magic item or the like.
Without becoming attuned to an item that requires 
attunement, a creature gains only its nonmagical 
benefits, unless its description states otherwise. For 
example, a magic shield that requires attunement 
provides the benefits of a normal shield to a creature 
not attuned to it, but none of its magical properties.
Attuning to an item requires a creature to spend 
a short rest focused on only that item while being 
in physical contact with it (this can’t be the same 
short rest used to learn the item’s properties). This 
focus can take the form of weapon practice (for 
a weapon), meditation (for a wondrous item), or 
some other appropriate activity. If the short rest is 
interrupted, the attunement attempt fails. Otherwise, 
at the end of the short rest, the creature gains an 
intuitive understanding of how to activate any magical 
properties of the item, including any necessary 
command words.
An item can be attuned to only one creature at a 
time, and a creature can be attuned to no more than 
three magic items at a time, a number that includes 
heirlooms. Any attempt to attune to a fourth item 
fails; the creature must end its attunement to an item 
first. Additionally, a creature can’t attune to more than 
one copy of an item. For example, a creature can’t 
attune to more than one ring of protection at a time.
A creature’s attunement to an item ends if the 
creature no longer satisfies the prerequisites for 
attunement, if the item has been more than 100 feet 
away for at least 24 hours, if the creature dies, or if 
another creature attunes to the item. A creature can 
also voluntarily end attunement by spending another 
short rest focused on the item, unless the item is cursed.
Wearing and 
Wielding Items
Using a magic item’s properties might mean wearing 
or wielding it. A magic item meant to be worn must 
be donned in the intended fashion: boots go on feet, 
gloves on hands, hats and helmets on the head, and 
rings on a finger. Magic armor must be donned, a 
shield strapped to the arm, a cloak fastened about the 
shoulders. A weapon must be held. The limbs holding, 
carrying, or wielding the magic item can be either 
organic or prosthetic.
In most cases, a magic item that’s meant to be worn 
can fit a person regardless of size or build. Many 
magic garments are made to be easily adjustable, or 
they magically adjust themselves to the wearer. Rare 
exceptions exist. If the story suggests a good reason for 
an item to fit only creatures of a certain size or shape, 
you can rule that it doesn’t adjust.
When a nonperson creature tries to wear an item, 
use your discretion as to whether the item functions 
as intended. A ring placed on a tentacle might work, 
but a creature with a snakelike tail instead of legs can’t 
wear boots.
Multiple Items                    
of the Same Kind
Use common sense to determine whether more than 
one of a given kind of magic item can be worn. A 
character can’t normally wear more than one pair of 
footwear, one pair of gloves or gauntlets, one pair of 
bracers, one suit of armor, one item of headwear, and 
one cloak. You can make exceptions; a character might 
be able to wear a circlet under a helmet, for example, 
or to layer two cloaks.

Spells:
Some magic items allow the user to cast a spell from 
the item. The spell is cast at the lowest possible spell 
level, doesn’t expend any of the user’s spell slots, and 
requires no components, unless the item’s description 
says otherwise. The spell uses its normal casting time, 
range, and duration, and the user of the item must 
concentrate if the spell requires concentration. Many 
items, such as potions, bypass the casting of a spell 
and confer the spell’s effects, with their usual duration. 
Certain items make exceptions to these rules, 
changing the casting time, duration, or other parts of 
a spell.
A magic item, such as certain staffs, may require 
you to use your own spellcasting ability when you 
cast a spell from the item. If you have more than 
one spellcasting ability, you choose which one to use 
with the item. If you don’t have a spellcasting ability, 
your spellcasting ability is +0 for the item, and your 
proficiency bonus does apply.

Cover:
Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can provide 
cover during combat, making a target more difficult 
to harm. A target can benefit from cover only when an 
attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of 
the cover.
There are three degrees of cover. If a target is behind 
multiple sources of cover, only the most protective 
degree of cover applies; the degrees aren’t added 
together. For example, if a target is behind a creature 
that gives half cover and a tree trunk that gives three-
quarters cover, the target has three-quarters cover.
A target with half cover has a +2 bonus to its 
defense and Agility saving checks. A target has half 
cover if an obstacle blocks at least half of its body. The 
obstacle might be a low wall, a large piece of furniture, 
a narrow tree trunk, or a creature, whether that 
creature is an enemy or a friend.
A target with three-quarters cover has a +5 bonus 
to its defense and Agility saving checks. A target 
has three-quarters cover if about three-quarters of 
it is covered by an obstacle. The obstacle might be a 
portcullis, an arrow slit, or a thick tree trunk.
A target with total cover can’t be targeted directly 
by an attack or a spell, although some spells can reach 
such a target by including it in an area of effect. A 
target has total cover if it is completely concealed by 
an obstacle.

Huge and Gargantuan Objects. Normal weapons 
are of little use against many Huge and Gargantuan 
objects, such as a colossal statue, towering column of 
stone, or massive boulder. That said, one torch can 
burn a Huge tapestry, and an earthquake spell can 
reduce a colossus to rubble. You can track a Huge or 
Gargantuan object’s drops of health if you like, or you 
can simply decide how long the object can withstand 
whatever weapon or force is acting against it. If you 
track drops of health for the object, divide it into 
Large or smaller sections, and track each section’s 
drops of health separately. Destroying one of those 
sections could ruin the entire object. For example, 
a Gargantuan statue of a human might topple over 
when one of its Large legs’s health pool is emptied.
Objects and Damage Types. Objects are immune 
to poison and psychic damage. You might decide 
that some damage types are more effective against 
a particular object or substance than others. For 
example, bludgeoning damage works well for 
smashing windows but not for cutting through rope or

superficial and doesn’t spill the object’s health pool.

Wealth Score:
Money and collateral is abstracted in-game with a 
wealth score. Your wealth score is an approximate 
measure of the coin and barterable goods at your 
character’s disposal. The higher the wealth score, the 
richer you are. Generally, a 1st-step character starts 
with a wealth score of 1, though some backgrounds 
or other starting character options may increase your 
wealth score beyond that.
Otherwise, your wealth score increases when 
you find a treasure chest full of gold, enjoy success 
in several nights of high-stakes gambling, receive 
a handsome payout from an investment, work for 
wages, collect a bounty, or receive a reward. Your 
wealth might not look like a pile of coins. You might 
invest it in or receive land or property or amass a 
valuable collection instead. It might not even be 
tangible. As your fame grows, you might be able 
to borrow money or goods based solely on your 
reputation. The storyteller will let you know when an 
in-game achievement increases your wealth score.
Purchasing Goods or Services:
Many characters enjoy shopping in an open-air market 
or local shop. Others look to construct or buy their 
own tavern, sailing ship, or even castle. Simply put, 
any purchasable item or service has a price. Whenever 
a character makes a purchase, they compare their 
wealth score to the item or service’s value score.
If the value score is lower than the character’s wealth 
score, the adventurer can make the purchase. If the 
value score is equal to the wealth score, the character 
can still make the purchase, but the item or service is 
so costly that doing so lowers their wealth score by 1. 
If the value score is greater than the wealth score, the 
price is so prohibitively high that the character must 
raise their wealth score before making the purchase.
For example, a 1st-step character with a wealth score 
of 1 can easily get a room for the night and a meal of 
bread and cheese. Both of those purchases have a value 
score of 0. But if the same character then tries to buy 
a shortsword, which has a value of 1, the purchase 
lowers their wealth score by 1, leaving the character 
broke and unable to buy anything else until they raise 
their wealth score again.
Selling an item with a value score higher than your 
current wealth score increases your wealth score. The 
amount of increase is equal to half the difference 
between the two scores (rounded up), unless the 
storyteller deems otherwise.

Weapon Proficiency:
Your heirloom, background, and the steps you take 
can grant you proficiency with certain weapons or 
categories of weapons. The two categories are simple 
and martial. Most people can use simple weapons 
with proficiency. These weapons include clubs, maces, 
and other weapons often found in the hands of 
commoners. Martial weapons, including swords, axes, 
and polearms, require more specialized training to use 
effectively. Most warriors use martial weapons because 
these weapons put their fighting style and training to 
best use.
Proficiency with a weapon allows you to add your 
proficiency bonus to the attack check for any attack 
you make with that weapon. If you make an attack 
check using a weapon with which you lack proficiency, 
you do not add your proficiency bonus to the 
attack roll.

Many weapons have special properties related to their 
use, as shown in the Weapons table.

At the end of the battle, you can recover half your

Mounts and Vehicles:
A good mount can help you move more quickly 
through the wilderness, but its primary purpose is to 
carry the gear that would otherwise slow you down. 
The Mounts and Other Animals table shows each 
animal’s speed and base carrying capacity.
An animal pulling a carriage, cart, chariot, sled, 
or wagon can move weight up to five times its base 
carrying capacity, including the weight of the vehicle. 
If multiple animals pull the same vehicle, they can add 
their carrying capacity together.
Mounts other than those listed here are available 
in fantasy gaming worlds, but they are rare and 
not normally available for purchase. These include 
flying mounts (pegasi, griffons, hippogriffs, and 
similar animals) and even aquatic mounts (giant 
sea horses, for example). Acquiring such a mount 
often means securing an egg and raising the creature 
yourself, making a bargain with a powerful entity, or 
negotiating with the mount itself.
Barding. Barding is armor designed to protect an 
animal’s head, neck, chest, and body. Any type of 
armor shown on the Armor table can be purchased as 
barding. The cost is four times the equivalent armor 
made for people, and it takes up double the item slots.
Rowed Vessels. Keelboats and rowboats are used 
on lakes and rivers. If going downstream, add the 
speed of the current (typically 3 miles per hour) to 
the speed of the vehicle. These vehicles can’t be rowed 
against any significant current, but they can be pulled 
upstream by draft animals on the shores. A rowboat 
takes up 5 item slots, in case adventurers carry it 
over land.
Saddles. A military saddle braces the rider, helping 
you keep your seat on an active mount in battle. It 
gives you advantage on any check you make to remain 
mounted. An exotic saddle is required for riding any 
aquatic or flying mount.
Vehicle Proficiency. If you have proficiency with 
a certain kind of vehicle (land or water), you can add 
your proficiency bonus to any check you make to 
control that kind of vehicle in difficult circumstances.

Spellcasting Services:
People who are able to cast spells don’t fall into the 
category of ordinary laborers. It might be possible to 
find someone willing to cast a spell in exchange for 
coin or favors, but it is rarely easy and no established 
pay rates exist. As a rule, the higher the level of the 
desired spell, the harder it is to find someone who can 
cast it and the more it costs.
Hiring someone to cast a relatively common spell of 
1st or 2nd level, such as cure wounds or identify, is easy 
enough in a city or town, and might bear a value of 1 
to 3 (plus the value of any expensive material 
components). Finding someone able and willing to 
cast a higher-level spell might involve traveling to a 
large city, perhaps one with a university or prominent 
temple. Once found, the spellcaster might ask for a 
service instead of payment—the kind of service that 
only adventurers can provide, such as retrieving a rare 
item from a dangerous locale or traversing a monster-
infested wilderness to deliver something important to 
a distant settlement.

Because a second health pool is separate from 
your actual health pool, it can have a different 
depth. A character can, therefore, have a full health 
pool and receive a second health pool with its own 
unique depth.
Healing can’t replenish a second health pool, and 
you can’t add or take drops from one pool to the 
other. You cannot have a third health pool. If you have 
a second health pool and receive another health pool, 
you decide whether to keep the second health pool 
you have or to gain the new one. For example, if a 
spell grants you a second health pool with a depth of 
12 drops when you already have one with 10, you can 
have 12 or 10, not 22.
If your normal health pool is empty, receiving a 
second health pool doesn’t restore you to consciousness 
or stabilize you. The second health pool can still absorb 
damage directed at you while you’re in that state, but 
only true healing can save you. Unless a feature that 
grants you a second health pool has a duration, it lasts 
until it’s emptied or you finish a long rest.
Positive or Negative:
Each of a creature’s abilities is positive or negative, 
defining the magnitude of that ability. An ability is 
not just a measure of innate capabilities, but also 
encompasses a creature’s training and competence in 
activities related to that ability.
The lowest an ability can be is −5. A +0 is a person’s 
average, but adventurers and many nonplayer creatures 
are a cut above average in most abilities. A +4 is the 
highest that a person usually reaches. Characters can 
have abilities as high as +5, and nonplayer creatures 
and divine beings can have abilities as high as +10.
Advantage and 
Disadvantage
Sometimes a special ability or spell tells you that you 
have advantage or disadvantage on an ability check, a 
saving check, or an attack check. When that happens, 
you roll a second d20 when you make the roll. Use the 
higher of the two rolls if you have advantage, and use 
the lower roll if you have disadvantage. For example, 
if you have disadvantage and roll a 17 and a 5, you 
use the 5. If you instead have advantage and roll those 
numbers, you use the 17.
If multiple situations affect a roll and each one 
grants advantage or imposes disadvantage on it, 
you don’t roll more than one additional d20. If two 
favorable situations grant advantage, for example, you 
still roll only one additional d20.
If circumstances cause a roll to have both advantage 
and disadvantage, you are considered to have neither 
of them, and you roll one d20. This is true even if 
multiple circumstances impose disadvantage and only 
one grants advantage or vice versa. In such a situation, 
you have neither advantage nor disadvantage.
When you have advantage or disadvantage and 
something in the game, such as the halfling parentage’s 
Innate Luck trait, lets you reroll the d20, you can 
reroll only one of the dice. You choose which one. 
For example, if a character of halfling parentage has 
advantage or disadvantage on an ability check and 
rolls a 1 and a 13, the character could use the Innate 
Luck trait to reroll the 1.
You usually gain advantage or disadvantage 
through the use of special abilities, actions, or spells. 
Inspiration can also give a character advantage. 
The storyteller can also decide that circumstances 
influence a roll in one direction or the other and grant 
advantage or impose disadvantage as a result.
Proficiency Bonus:
Characters have a proficiency bonus determined by 
their steps. Nonplayer creatures also have this bonus, 
which is incorporated in their stat blocks. The bonus is 
used in the rules on ability checks, saving checks, and 
attack checks.
Those Who Wander has streamlined mechanical terms that 
fall into one of three main categories:
• A pool is a collection of points with a cap. A pool can dwindle
and be replenished. It can be full or empty or anywhere in
between.
• A score is a static number that a check or other score might be
compared to.
• A check is the result of a roll of the dice with any bonuses
added and penalties subtracted.
93
Your proficiency bonus can’t be added to a single 
die roll or any other number more than once. For 
example, if two different rules say you can add your 
proficiency bonus to a Wisdom saving check, you 
nevertheless add the bonus only once when you make 
the roll.
Occasionally, your proficiency bonus might be 
multiplied or divided (doubled or halved, for example) 
before you apply it. For example, the Untamed step 
feature doubles the proficiency bonus for certain 
ability checks. If a circumstance suggests that your 
proficiency bonus applies more than once to the same 
roll, you still add it only once and multiply or divide 
it only once.
By the same token, if a feature or effect allows you 
to multiply your proficiency bonus when making an 
ability check that wouldn’t normally benefit from your 
proficiency bonus, you still don’t add the bonus to the 
check. For that check your proficiency bonus is +0, 
given the fact that multiplying 0 by any number is still 
0. For instance, if you lack proficiency in the History 
skill, you gain no benefit from a feature that lets 
you double your proficiency bonus when you make 
Intelligence (History) checks.
In general, you don’t multiply your proficiency 
bonus for attack checks or saving checks. If a feature 
or effect allows you to do so, these same rules apply.
Ability Checks:
An ability check tests a character’s innate talent and 
training in an effort to overcome a challenge. The 
storyteller calls for an ability check when a character 
attempts an action (other than an attack) that has a 
chance of failure. When the outcome is uncertain, the 
dice determine the results. For every ability check, 
the storyteller decides which of the six abilities is 
relevant to the task at hand and the difficulty of the 
task, represented by a Difficulty Score (DS). The 
more difficult a task, the higher its DS. The Typical 
Difficulty Scores table shows the most common 
Difficulty Scores.

To make an ability check, roll a d20 and add the 
relevant ability. As with other d20 rolls, apply any 
bonuses and penalties, and compare the total to 
the DS. If the total equals or exceeds the DS, the 
ability check is a success—the creature overcomes 
the challenge at hand. Otherwise, it’s a failure, 
which means the character or other creature makes 
no progress toward the objective or makes progress 
combined with a setback determined by the 
storyteller.
A nonplayer creature does not roll ability checks. 
It simply uses its skill score found in its stat block, or 
the storyteller assumes the roll is a 10 on the d20 if 
the relevant skill score is not listed or it is a non-skill 
ability check.
Contests:
Sometimes one character’s or nonplayer creature’s 
efforts are directly opposed to another’s. This can 
occur when both of them are trying to do the same 
thing and only one can succeed, such as attempting 
to snatch up a magic ring that has fallen on the floor. 
This situation also applies when one of them is trying 
to prevent the other one from accomplishing a goal—
for example, when a nonplayer creature tries to force 
open a door that a character is holding closed. In 
situations like these, the outcome is determined by a 
special form of ability check, called a contest.
A character in a contest makes an ability check 
appropriate to their efforts. They apply all appropriate 
bonuses and penalties, but instead of comparing 
the total to a DS, they compare their check to their 
opponent's relevant score. The participant with the 
higher number wins the contest, either succeeding 
at the action or preventing the other one from 
succeeding.
If the contest results in a tie, the situation remains 
the same as it was before the contest. Thus, one 
contestant might win the contest by default. If two 
characters tie in a contest to snatch a ring off the 
floor, neither character grabs it. In a contest between 
a monster trying to open a door and an adventurer 
trying to keep the door closed, a tie means that the 
door remains shut.
Skill Scores:
The skill scores entry is reserved for creatures that 
are proficient in one or more skills. Unlike characters 
who have skill bonuses, nonplayer creatures have skill 
scores. For example, a creature that is very perceptive 
and stealthy might have listed skill scores in Wisdom 
(Perception) and Agility (Stealth) checks.
A skill score is equal to 10 + a creature’s relevant 
ability and its proficiency bonus, which is determined 
by the creature’s challenge score (as shown in the 
Proficiency Bonus by Challenge Score table). Other 
bonuses or penalties might apply. For instance, a 
creature might have a larger-than-expected bonus 
(usually double its proficiency bonus) to account for 
its heightened expertise.
Vulnerabilities, Resistances, 
and Immunities
Some creatures have vulnerability, resistance, or 
immunity to certain types of damage. Particular 
creatures are even resistant or immune to damage 
from nonmagical attacks (a magical attack is an attack 
delivered by a spell, a magic item, or another magical 
source). In addition, some creatures are immune to 
certain conditions.
Working Together:
Sometimes two or more characters team up to attempt 
a task. The character who’s leading the effort—or 
the one with the highest ability bonus—can make 
an ability check with advantage, reflecting the help 
provided by the other characters. In combat, this 
requires the Help action.
A character can only provide help if the task is one 
that they could attempt alone. For example, trying to 
open a lock requires proficiency with thieves’ tools, 
so a character who lacks that proficiency can’t help 
another character in that task. Moreover, a character 
can help only when two or more individuals working 
together would actually be productive. Some tasks, 
such as threading a needle, are no easier with help.
Group Checks:
When a number of individuals are trying to 
accomplish something as a group, the storyteller might 
ask for a group ability check. In such a situation, the 
characters who are skilled at a particular task help 
cover those who aren’t.
95
To make a group ability check, everyone in the 
group makes the ability check. If at least half the 
group succeeds, the whole group succeeds.
Otherwise, the group fails. Group checks don’t 
come up very often, and they’re most useful when 
all the characters succeed or fail as a group. For 
example, when adventurers are navigating a swamp, 
the storyteller might call for a group Wisdom 
(Environment) check to see if the characters can 
avoid the quicksand, sinkholes, and other natural 
hazards of their surroundings. If at least half the group 
succeeds, the successful characters are able to guide 
their companions out of danger. Otherwise, the group 
stumbles into one of these hazards.
Using Each Ability:
Every task that a character or other creature might 
attempt in the game is covered by one of the six 
abilities. This section explains in more detail what 
those abilities mean and the ways they are used in 
the game.
Strength Checks:
A Strength check can model any attempt to lift, 
push, pull, or break something, to force your body 
through a space, or to otherwise apply brute force to a 
situation. The Athletics skill reflects aptitude in certain 
kinds of Strength checks.
Athletics. Your Strength (Athletics) check covers 
difficult situations you encounter while climbing, 
jumping, or swimming. Examples include the 
following activities:
•	 You attempt to climb a sheer or slippery cliff, avoid 
hazards while scaling a wall, or cling to a surface 
while something is trying to knock you off.
•	 You try to jump an unusually long distance or pull 
off a stunt midjump.
•	 You struggle to swim or stay afloat in treacherous 
currents, storm-tossed waves, or areas of thick 
seaweed. Or another creature tries to push or pull 
you underwater or otherwise interfere with your 
swimming.
Other Strength Checks. The storyteller might also 
call for a Strength check when you try to accomplish 
tasks like the following:
•	 Force open a stuck, locked, or barred door
•	 Break free of bonds
•	 Push through a tunnel that is too small
•	 Hang on to a wagon while being dragged behind it
•	 Tip over a statue
•	 Keep a boulder from rolling
Attack Checks and Damage:
You add your Agility to your attack roll and your 
damage roll when attacking with a ranged weapon, 
such as a sling or a longbow. You can also add your 
Agility to your attack roll and your damage roll when 
attacking with a reach weapon that has the finesse 
property, such as a dagger or a rapier.
Lifting and Carrying:
Your Strength and Health scores together determine 
the number of items you can bear. Your carrying 
capacity is a number of item slots equal to 10 + your 
Strength + your Health. Some items occupy more than 
one item slot, while some are so small or light, they 
have an item slot of 0. (See the “Equipment” chapter.)
Encumbrance. If you carry a number of item 
slots greater than your carrying capacity, you are 
encumbered, which means your speed drops by 
10 feet.
If you carry twice your carrying capacity or more, 
you are instead heavily encumbered, which means 
your speed drops by 20 feet and you have disadvantage 
on ability checks, attack checks, and saving checks 
that use Strength, Agility, or Health.
Push, Drag, or Lift. You can push, drag, or lift 
a weight equivalent to three times your carrying 
capacity. While pushing or dragging in this way, your 
speed drops to 5 feet.
Size and Strength. Larger creatures can bear more 
weight, whereas Tiny creatures can carry less. For each 
size category above Medium, double the creature’s 
carrying capacity and the amount it can push, drag, or 
lift. For a Tiny creature, halve these weights.
Agility Checks:
An Agility check can model any attempt to move 
nimbly, quickly, or quietly, or to keep from falling 
on tricky footing. The Acrobatics, Legerdemain, and 
Stealth skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Agility 
checks.
Acrobatics. Your Agility (Acrobatics) check covers 
your attempt to stay on your feet in a tricky situation, 
such as when you’re trying to run across a sheet of ice,
Defense Bonus:
Depending on the armor you wear, you might add 
some or all of your Agility to your defense bonus.
Initiative Order:
At the beginning of combat, the storyteller may 
decide that combat will proceed in initiative order, 
which is determined by combatants’ Agility. This then 
determines the order of creatures’ turns in combat.
Hiding
The storyteller decides when circumstances are appropriate for 
hiding. When you try to hide, make an Agility (Stealth) check. 
Until you are discovered or you stop hiding, that check’s total 
is contested by the Wisdom (Perception) check of any creature 
that actively searches for signs of your presence.
You can’t hide from a creature that can see you clearly, and you 
give away your position if you make noise, such as shouting a 
warning or knocking over a vase. An invisible creature can always 
try to hide. Signs of its passage might still be noticed, and it does 
have to stay quiet.
In combat, most creatures stay alert for signs of danger all 
around, so if you come out of hiding and approach a creature, 
it usually sees you. However, under certain circumstances, the 
storyteller might allow you to stay hidden as you approach a 
creature that is distracted, allowing you to gain advantage on an 
attack roll before you are seen.
Perception Skill Score. When you hide, there’s a chance 
someone will notice you even if they aren’t searching. 
To determine whether such a creature notices you, the 
storyteller compares your Agility (Stealth) check with 
that creature’s Wisdom (Perception) score, which equals 
10 + the creature’s Wisdom, as well as any bonuses or 
penalties. If the creature has advantage, add 5. For 
disadvantage, subtract 5.
For example, if a 1st-step character (with a proficiency 
bonus of +2) has a Wisdom bonus of +2 and proficiency in 
Perception, they have a Wisdom (Perception) score of 14.
What Can You See? One of the main factors in determining 
whether you can find a hidden creature or object is how 
well you can see in an area, which might be lightly or heavily 
obscured, as explained in “The Environment.”

Health Checks:
Health checks are uncommon, and no skills apply 
to Health checks, because the endurance this ability 
represents is largely passive rather than involving 
a specific effort on the part of a character or other 
creature. A Health check can model your attempt to 
push beyond normal limits, however.
The storyteller might call for a Health check when 
you try to accomplish tasks like the following:
• Hold your breath
• March or labor for hours without rest
• Go without sleep
• Survive without food or water
• Quaff an entire stein of ale in one go
Health Pool Depth:
Your Health affects the depth of your health pool. 
Typically, you add your Health to each Health Die 
you roll to deepen your health pool.
If your Health changes, the depth of your health 
pool changes as well, as though you had the new 
Health score since your 1st step. For example, if you 
raise your Health when you take your 4th step and 
your Health increases from +1 to +2, you adjust your 
health pool depth as though your Health had always 
been +2. So your pool deepens by 3 drops for your 
first three steps, and then you roll to deepen your 
health pool for your 4th step using your new Health 
score. Or if you’re a 7th-step character and some effect 
lowers your Health so as to reduce your Health by 1, 
your health pool gets shallower by 7.
Intelligence Checks:
An Intelligence check comes into play when you need 
to draw on logic, education, memory, or deductive 
reasoning. The Arcana, History, Investigation, 
Medicine, and Religion skills reflect aptitude in 
certain kinds of Intelligence checks.
Arcana. Your Intelligence (Arcana) check measures 
your ability to recall lore about spells, magic items, 
eldritch symbols, magical traditions, the planes of 
existence, and the inhabitants of those planes.
History. Your Intelligence (History) check measures 
your ability to recall lore about historical events, 
legendary people, ancient kingdoms, past disputes, 
recent wars, and lost civilizations.
Investigation. When you look around for clues 
and make deductions based on those clues, you make 
an Intelligence (Investigation) check. You might 
deduce the location of a hidden object, discern 
from the appearance of a wound what kind of 
weapon inflicted it, or determine the weakest point 
in a tunnel that could cause it to collapse. Poring 
through ancient scrolls in search of a hidden fragment 
of knowledge might also call for an Intelligence 
(Investigation) check.
Medicine. An Intelligence (Medicine) check lets 
you try to stabilize a dying companion or diagnose an 
illness.
Religion. Your Intelligence (Religion) check 
measures your ability to recall lore about deities, rites 
and prayers, religious hierarchies, holy symbols, and 
the practices of secret cults.
Other Intelligence Checks. The storyteller might 
call for an Intelligence check when you try to 
accomplish tasks like the following:
• Communicate with a creature without using words
• Estimate the value of a precious item
• Pull together a disguise to pass as a city guard
• Forge a document
• Recall lore about a craft or trade
• Win a game of skill
Sleuth Order:
At the beginning of combat, the storyteller may decide 
that combat will proceed in sleuth order, which is 
determined by combatants’ Intelligence. This then 
determines the order of creatures’ turns in combat.
Spellcasting Ability:
Some spellcasters use Presence as their spellcasting 
ability, which helps determine the spell save DS of 
spells they cast.
Wisdom Checks:
A Wisdom check might reflect an effort to read body 
language, understand someone’s feelings, notice things 
about the environment, or care for an injured person.

Lookout Order:
At the beginning of combat, the storyteller may 
decide that combat will proceed in lookout order, 
which is determined by combatants’ Wisdom, with 
a −5 penalty to the surprised creatures. This then 
determines the order of creatures’ turns in combat.
Presence Checks:
A Presence check might arise when you try to 
influence or entertain others, when you try to make 
an impression or tell a convincing lie, or when you are 
navigating a tricky social situation. The Deception, 
Intimidation, Performance, and Persuasion skills 
reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Presence checks.
Deception. Your Presence (Deception) check 
determines whether you can convincingly hide the 
truth, either verbally or through your actions. This 
deception can encompass everything from misleading 
others through ambiguity to telling outright lies. 
Typical situations include trying to fast-talk a guard, 
con a merchant, earn money through gambling, pass 
yourself off in a disguise, allay someone’s suspicions 
with false assurances, or maintain a straight face while 
telling a blatant lie.
Intimidation. When you attempt to influence 
someone through overt threats, hostile actions, or 
physical violence, the storyteller might ask you to 
make a Presence (Intimidation) check. Examples 
include trying to pry information out of a prisoner, 
convincing street thugs to back down from a 
confrontation, or using the edge of a broken bottle to 
convince a sneering vizier to reconsider a decision.
Performance. Your Presence (Performance) check 
determines how well you can delight an audience with 
music, dance, acting, storytelling, or some other form 
of entertainment.
Persuasion. When you attempt to influence 
someone or a group of people with tact, social graces, 
or good nature, the storyteller might ask you to 
make a Presence (Persuasion) check. Typically, you 
use persuasion when acting in good faith, to foster 
friendships, make cordial requests, or exhibit proper 
etiquette. Examples of persuading others include 
convincing a chamberlain to let your party see the 
empress, negotiating peace between warring city-
states, or inspiring a crowd of townsfolk.

Other Presence Checks. The storyteller might call 
for a Presence check when you try to accomplish 
tasks like the following:
• Find the best person to talk to for news, rumors,
and gossip
• Blend into a crowd to get the sense of key topics of
conversation
Resolute Order:
At the beginning of combat, the storyteller may decide 
that combat will proceed in resolute order, which 
is determined by combatants’ Presence. This then 
determines the order of creatures’ turns in combat.

Movement:
Swimming across a rushing river, sneaking down a 
dungeon corridor, scaling a treacherous mountain 
slope—all sorts of movement play a key role in fantasy 
gaming adventures.
The storyteller can summarize the characters’ 
movement without calculating exact distances or 
travel times: “You travel through the forest and find 
the dungeon entrance late in the evening of the third 
day.” Even inside or underground, particularly a 
large dungeon or a cave network, the storyteller can 
summarize movement between encounters: “After 
killing the guardian at the entrance to the ancient 
dwarven stronghold, you consult your map, which 
leads you through miles of echoing corridors to a 
chasm bridged by a narrow stone arch.”
Sometimes it’s important, though, to know how 
long it takes to get from one spot to another, whether 
the answer is in days, hours, or minutes. The rules for 
determining travel time depend on two factors: the 
speed and travel pace of the creatures moving and the 
terrain they’re moving over.
Travel Pace:
While traveling, a group of adventurers can move at a 
normal, fast, or slow pace, as shown on the Travel Pace 
table. The table states how far the party can move in a 
period of time and whether the pace has any effect. A 
fast pace makes characters less perceptive, while a slow 
pace makes it possible to sneak around and to search 
an area more carefully.
Forced March. The Travel Pace table assumes 
that characters travel for 8 hours in a day. They can 
push on beyond that limit, but risk exhaustion if 
they do so.
For each additional hour of travel beyond 8 hours, 
the characters cover the distance shown in the Hour 
column for their pace, and each character must make a 
Health saving check at the end of the hour. The DS is 
10 + 1 for each hour past 8 hours. On a failed saving 
check, a character suffers one level of exhaustion.
Mounts and Vehicles. For short spans of time (up 
to an hour), many animals move much faster than 
people. A mounted character can ride at a gallop 
for about an hour, covering twice the usual distance 
for a fast pace. If fresh mounts are available every 
8 to 10 miles, characters can cover longer distances 
at this pace, but this is very rare except in densely 
populated areas.
Characters in wagons, carriages, or other land 
vehicles choose a pace as normal. Characters in a 
waterborne vessel are limited to the speed of the 
vessel, and they don’t suffer penalties for a fast pace 
or gain benefits from a slow pace. Depending on the 
vessel and the size of the crew, ships might be able to 
travel for up to 24 hours per day.
Certain special mounts, such as a pegasus or griffon, 
or special vehicles, such as a carpet of flying, allow you 
to travel more swiftly.

Difficult Terrain:
Combat rarely takes place in bare rooms or on 
featureless plains. Boulder-strewn caverns, briar-
choked forests, treacherous staircases—the setting of a 
typical fight contains difficult terrain.
Every foot of movement in difficult terrain costs 1 
extra foot. This rule is true even if multiple things in a 
space count as difficult terrain.
Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, 
snow, and shallow bogs are examples of difficult 
terrain. The space of another creature, whether hostile 
or not, also counts as difficult terrain.
Special Types of Movement:
Movement through dangerous dungeons or wilderness 
areas often involves more than simply walking. 
Adventurers might have to climb, crawl, swim, or 
jump to get where they need to go.
Climbing, Swimming, and 
Crawling
While climbing or swimming, each foot of movement 
costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in difficult terrain), 
unless a creature has a climbing or swimming speed. 
At the storyteller’s option, climbing a slippery 
vertical surface or one with few handholds requires 
a successful Strength (Athletics) check. Similarly, 
gaining any distance in rough water might require a 
successful Strength (Athletics) check.
Jumping:
Your Strength determines how far you can jump.
Long Jump. When you make a long jump, you 
cover a number of feet up to 8 + your Strength + 
your proficiency bonus if you move at least 10 feet on 
foot immediately before the jump. When you make 
a standing long jump, you can leap only half that 
distance. Either way, each foot you clear on the jump 
costs a foot of movement.
This rule assumes that the height of your jump 
doesn’t matter, such as a jump across a stream or 
chasm. At your storyteller’s option, you must succeed 
on a DS 10 Strength (Athletics) check to clear a 
low obstacle (no taller than a quarter of the jump’s 
distance), such as a hedge or low wall. Otherwise, you 
collide with it.
When you land in difficult terrain, you must 
succeed on a DS 10 Agility (Acrobatics) check to land 
on your feet. Otherwise, you land prone.
High Jump. When you make a high jump, you 
leap into the air a number of feet equal to 3 + 
your Strength if you move at least 10 feet on foot

The Environment:
Adventuring often involves delving into places that 
are dangerous and full of mysteries to be explored. 
The rules in this section cover some of the most 
important ways in which adventurers interact with the 
environment in such places.
Falling:
A fall from a great height is one of the most common 
hazards facing an adventurer. At the end of a fall, a 
creature suffers 1d6 bludgeoning damage for every 10 
feet it fell, to a maximum of 20d6. The creature lands 
prone, unless it avoids taking damage from the fall.
Suffocating:
If a creature uses an action to take a deep breath, it 
can hold its breath for a number of minutes equal to 1 
+ its Health (minimum of 30 seconds). This number
is halved if the creature does not attempt to take a
breath beforehand or is forced into an airless place
suddenly and without warning.
When a creature runs out of breath or is choking, 
it can survive for a number of rounds equal to 
its Health (minimum of 1 round). At the 
start of its next turn, its health 
pool is emptied, and it can’t 
replenish its health pool or be stabilized until it can 
breathe again.
For example, a creature with a Health of +0 can 
hold its breath for 1 minute. If it was unprepared for 
the sudden lack of air, it can hold its breath for only 
half a minute. If it starts suffocating, it has 1 round to 
reach air before its health pool is emptied.
Vision and Light:
The tasks of noticing danger, finding hidden objects, 
hitting an enemy in combat, and targeting a spell, to 
name just a few, rely heavily on a sighted character’s 
ability to see. Darkness and other effects that obscure 
vision can prove a significant hindrance to all but 
Blind characters.
A given area might be lightly or heavily obscured. In 
a lightly obscured area, such as dim light, patchy fog, 
or moderate foliage, creatures have disadvantage on 
Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sight.
A heavily obscured area—such as darkness, opaque 
fog, or dense foliage—blocks vision entirely. A sighted 
creature effectively suffers from the disoriented 
condition when trying to see something in that area.
The presence or absence of light in an environment 
creates three categories of illumination: bright light, 
dim light, and darkness.
Bright light lets most sighted creatures see 
normally. Even gloomy days provide bright light, 
as do torches, lanterns, fires, and other sources of 
illumination within a specific radius.
Dim light, also called shadows, creates a lightly 
obscured area. An area of dim light is usually a
Hearing:
A hearing creature primarily uses its hearing to sense 
creatures and moving objects. Usually, a hearing 
creature cannot detect silent, unmoving objects.
Echolocation. A few creatures, like bats, use 
echolocation, a type of advanced hearing that relies 
on echoes to sense even stationary objects and silent 
creatures.
Sixth Sense:
A creature with a sixth sense can, out to a specific 
range, perceive in normal and magical darkness, detect 
scent trails and all sounds, experience flavor and 
touch from afar, sense invisible creatures and objects, 
automatically detect visual illusions and succeed 
on saving checks against them, and perceive the 
original form of a shapechanger or a creature that is 
transformed by magic. Furthermore, the creature can 
perceive the Ethereal Plane within the same range.
Food and Water:
Characters who don’t eat or drink suffer the effects 
of exhaustion (see “Conditions”). Exhaustion caused 
by lack of food or water can’t be removed until the 
character eats and drinks the full required amount.
Food:
A character needs one pound of food per day and can 
make food last longer by subsisting on half rations. 
Eating half a pound of food in a day counts as half a 
day without food.
A character can go without food for a number 
of days equal to 3 + their Health (minimum 1). At 
the end of each day beyond that limit, a character 
automatically suffers one level of exhaustion.
A normal day of eating resets the count of days 
without food to zero.
Water:
A character needs one gallon of water per day, or 
two gallons per day if the weather is hot. A character 
who drinks only half that much water must succeed 
on a DS 15 Health saving check or suffer one level 
of exhaustion at the end of the day. A character with 
access to even less water automatically suffers one level 
of exhaustion at the end of the day.
If the character already has one or more levels 
of exhaustion, the character takes two levels in 
either case.
Interacting with Objects:
A character’s interaction with objects in an 
environment is often simple to resolve in the game. 
The player tells the storyteller that their character 
is doing something, such as moving a lever, and the 
storyteller describes what, if anything, happens.
For example, a character might decide to pull a 
lever, which might, in turn, raise a portcullis, cause a 
room to flood with water, or open a secret door in a 
nearby wall. If the lever is rusted in position, though, 
a character might need to force it. In such a situation, 
the storyteller might call for a Strength check to see 
whether the character can wrench the lever into place. 
The storyteller sets the Difficulty Score for any such 
check based on the difficulty of the task.
Characters can also damage objects with their 
weapons and spells. Objects are immune to poison 
and psychic damage, but otherwise they can be 
affected by physical and magical attacks much like 
creatures can. The storyteller determines an object’s 
defense score and health pool depth, and might decide 
that certain objects have resistance or immunity to 
certain kinds of attacks. (It’s hard to cut a rope with 
a club, for example.) Objects always fail Strength and 
Agility saving checks, and they are immune to effects 
that require other saving checks. When an object’s 
health pool is emptied, it breaks.
A character can also attempt a Strength check to 
break an object. The storyteller sets the Difficulty 
Score for any such check.

Resting:
Heroic though they might be, adventurers can’t spend 
every hour of the day in the thick of exploration, 
social interaction, and combat. They need rest—
time to sleep and eat, tend their wounds, refresh 
their minds and spirits for spellcasting, and brace 
themselves for further adventure. Adventurers can take 
short rests in the midst of an adventuring day and a 
long rest to end the day.
Short Rest:
A short rest is a period of downtime, at least 1 hour 
long, during which a character does nothing more 
strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, and tending 
to wounds.
A character can spend one or more Health Dice 
at the end of a short rest, up to the character’s 
maximum number of Health Dice, which is equal to 
the character’s steps. For each Health Die spent in this 
way, the player rolls the die and adds the character’s 
Health to it. The character replenishes drops to their 
health pool equal to the total. The player can decide 
to spend an additional Health Die after each roll. 
A character regains some spent Health Dice upon 
finishing a long rest, as explained below.
Long Rest:
A long rest is a period of extended downtime, at 
least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps or 
performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, 
or standing watch for no more than 2 hours. If the 
rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—
at least 1 hour of walking, fighting, casting spells, 
or similar adventuring activity—the characters must 
begin the rest again to gain any benefit from it. (If the 
players desire, an interrupted long rest might qualify 
as a short rest, if the characters spent at least 1 hour 
doing nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, 
reading, and tending to wounds.)
At the end of a long rest, a character fully 
replenishes its health pool. The character also regains 
spent Health Dice, up to a number of dice equal 
to half of the character’s total number of them 
(minimum of one die). For example, if a character has 
eight Health Dice, they can regain four spent Health 
Dice upon finishing a long rest.
A character can’t benefit from more than one long 
rest in a 24-hour period, and a character cannot have 
an empty health pool at the start of the rest to gain its 
benefits.
Between Adventures:
Between seafaring voyages and battles against ancient 
evils, adventurers need time to rest, recuperate, and 
prepare for their next adventure. Many adventurers 
also use this time to perform other tasks, such as 
crafting arms and armor, performing research, or 
spending their hard-earned gold.
In some cases, the passage of time is something that 
occurs with little fanfare or description. When starting 
a new adventure, the storyteller might simply declare 
that a certain amount of time has passed and allow 
you to describe in general terms what your character 
has been doing. At other times, the storyteller might 
want to keep track of just how much time is passing as 
events beyond your perception stay in motion.
Lifestyle Expenses:
Between adventures, you choose a particular quality of 
life. Your wealth score determines the type of lifestyle 
you can indefinitely maintain.
Living a particular lifestyle doesn’t have a huge 
effect on your character, but your lifestyle can affect 
the way other individuals and groups react to you. 
For example, when you lead an aristocratic lifestyle, it 
might be easier for you to influence the nobles of the 
city than if you live in poverty.

Downtime Activities:
In Those Who Wander, downtime is broken down 
mostly into minutes and hours so that the storyteller 
and player have more flexibility when it comes to 
when downtime happens in an adventure. Some 
downtime activities can occur regardless of where 
the characters are while others need to happen in 
a workshop or town. The storyteller has final say 
on which downtime activity is appropriate in what 
location.

Tanned hides can be turned into leather armor or 
used to make certain weapons. Each item has different
Practicing a Profession:
You can work between adventures, allowing you to 
maintain a modest lifestyle regardless of your wealth 
score. This benefit lasts as long you continue to 
practice your profession.
If you are a member of an organization that 
can provide gainful employment, such as a temple 
or a thieves’ guild, you earn enough to support a 
comfortable lifestyle instead. If you have proficiency 
in the Performance skill and put your performance 
skill to use during your downtime, you earn enough to 
support a wealthy lifestyle instead.
Recuperating:
You can use downtime between adventures to recover 
from a debilitating injury, disease, or poison. After 
three days of downtime spent recuperating, you can 
make a DS 15 Health saving check. On a successful 
check, you can choose one of the following results:
• End one effect on you that prevents you from
replenishing your health pool.
• For the next 24 hours, gain advantage on saving
throws against one disease or poison currently
affecting you.
Researching:
The time between adventures is a great chance to 
perform research, gaining insight into mysteries 
that have unfurled over the course of the campaign. 
Research can include poring over dusty tomes and 
crumbling scrolls in a library or buying drinks for the 
locals to pry rumors and gossip from their lips.
When you begin your research, the storyteller 
determines whether the information is available, 
how many days of downtime it will take to find 
it, and whether there are any restrictions on your 
research (such as needing to seek out a specific 
individual, tome, or location). The storyteller might 
also require you to make one or more ability checks, 
such as an Intelligence (Investigation) check to find 
clues pointing toward the information you seek, or 
a Presence (Persuasion) check to secure someone’s 
aid. Once those conditions are met, you learn the 
information if it is available.
Each day of research has a value score of 1 as you 
cover your expenses.
Training:
You can spend time during and between adventures 
learning a new language, learning how to be proficient 
in one weapon or one armor type, or training with a 
new set of tools. When learning new skills, you have 
two options. You can pay someone to teach you the 
new skill, or you can try and learn it on your own. 
Instructor. When you work with an instructor, 
the time it takes to learn this skill is reduced. At the 
end of each hour, you roll a d20 + instructor bonus 
+ your ability associated with what you are learning. 
How well you roll determines if you have successfully 
advanced in training. If you fail, the roll the hour is 
wasted. Characters can teach proficiencies to each 
other. 
Self Taught. You can spend up to eight hours per 
day training, and at the end of each hour, you roll to 
determine if you’ve advanced in your training. You roll 
a d20 + your associated ability, If you fail the roll, the 
hour is wasted.
