The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two 
sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, 
footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the 
chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. 
A round represents about 6 seconds in the game 
world. During a round, each participant in a battle 
takes a turn. The order of turns is determined at the 
105
beginning of a combat encounter, when the storyteller 
chooses one of four methods. Once everyone has 
taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if 
neither side has defeated the other or surrendered.
Combat Step by Step:
1.
Establish positions. The storyteller decides
where all the characters and nonplayer creatures
are located. Given the characters’ marching
order or their stated positions in the room or
other location, the storyteller figures out where
the adversaries are—how far away and in what
direction.
2.
Determine turn order. The storyteller chooses
one of four methods to determine the order of
combatants’ turns.
3.
Take turns. Each participant in the battle takes a
turn in order.
4.
Begin the next round. When everyone involved
in the combat has had a turn, the round ends.
Repeat step 3 until the fighting stops.
Turn Order:
The way in which you approach a fight greatly 
determines who gets the first turn.
The storyteller chooses from among one of four turn 
orders, which are detailed as follows:
• Initiative order. When both sides of combat are 
aware of each other and equally prepared for battle, 
who goes first is a matter of raw reflexes. If neither 
side tries to be stealthy or both sides fail their 
Agility (Stealth) checks, this is an appropriate order 
to follow. If the storyteller determines that initiative 
order is appropriate, turn order proceeds according 
to combatants’ Agility.
• Lookout order. The storyteller determines whether 
anyone involved in the combat encounter is 
surprised. When one side surprises the other, who 
goes first is a matter of perception. For example, a 
party of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, 
springing from the trees to attack them. Turn order 
proceeds according to combatants’ Wisdom, but 
each surprised creature receives a −5 penalty to its 
Wisdom for the purpose of determining turn order.
• Resolute order. In the face of terrible danger, who 
goes first is a matter of bravery and mettle. For 
example, the party might be staring down an 
ancient dragon. Using resolute order, turn order 
proceeds according to combatants’ Presence.
• Sleuth order. When combat is preceded by a battle 
of wits or sleuthing, who goes first is mind over 
matter. For example, the party could deduce the
duke was poisoned by a person still in the room. 
Using sleuth order, turn order proceeds according 
to combatants’ Intelligence.
When combat starts, the storyteller ranks the 
combatants in order from the one with the highest 
relevant ability to the one with the lowest ability. This 
is the order in which they act during each round. The 
turn order remains the same from round to round.
If there is a tie, the storyteller decides the order 
among tied nonplayer creatures, and the players decide 
the order among their tied characters. The storyteller 
can decide the order if the tie is between a nonplayer 
creature and a character. Optionally, the storyteller 
can have the tied characters and nonplayer creatures 
each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll 
going first.
Your Turn:
On your turn, you can move a distance up to your 
speed and take one action. You decide whether to 
move first or take your action first. Your speed—
sometimes called your overland speed—is noted on 
your character sheet.
The most common actions you can take are 
described in the “Actions in Combat” section later 
in this chapter. Many character features and other 
abilities provide additional options for your action. 
The “Movement and Position” section later in this 
chapter gives the rules for your move.
You can forgo moving, taking an action, or doing 
anything at all on your turn. If you can’t decide what 
to do on your turn, consider taking the Dodge or 
Ready action, as described in “Actions in Combat.”
Other Activity on Your Turn. Your turn can include 
a variety of flourishes that require neither your action 
nor your move.
You can communicate however you are able, 
through brief utterances and gestures, as you take 
your turn.
You can also interact with one object or feature of 
the environment for free, during either your move 
or your action. For example, you could open a door 
during your move as you stride toward a foe, or you 
could draw your weapon as part of the same action 
you use to attack.
If you want to interact with a second object, you 
need to use your action. Some magic items and other 
special objects always require an action to use, as 
stated in their descriptions.
The storyteller might require you to use an action 
for any of these activities when it needs special care 
or when it presents an unusual obstacle. For instance,
Reactions:
Shield. When a creature makes an attack against the 
wearer of the guardian’s amulet, the guardian grants 
a +2 bonus to the wearer’s defense if the guardian is 
within 5 feet of the wearer.
Movement and Position:
In combat, characters and nonplayer creatures are in 
constant motion, often using movement and position 
to gain the upper hand. On your turn, you can move 
a distance up to your speed. You can use as much or as 
little of your speed as you like on your turn, following 
the rules here.
Your movement can include jumping, climbing, and 
swimming. These different modes of movement can 
be combined with walking or wheeling, or they can 
constitute your entire move. However you’re moving, 
you deduct the distance of each part of your move 
from your speed until it is used up or until you are 
done moving.
Breaking Up Your Move:
You can break up your movement on your turn, using 
some of your speed before and after your action. For 
example, if you have a speed of 30 feet, you can move 
10 feet, take your action, and then move 20 feet.
If you take an action that includes more than one 
weapon attack, you can break up your movement even 
further by moving between those attacks. For example, 
a character who takes the Swift step feature and who 
has a speed of 25 feet could move 10 feet, make an 
attack, move 15 feet, and then attack again.
If you have more than one speed, such as your 
overland speed and a flying speed, you can switch 
back and forth between your speeds during your 
move. Whenever you switch, subtract the distance 
you’ve already moved from the new speed. The result 
determines how much farther you can move. If the 
result is 0 or less, you can’t use the new speed during 
the current move.
For example, if you have a speed of 30 and a flying 
speed of 60 because a mage cast the fly spell on you, 
you could fly 20 feet, then walk or wheel 10 feet, and 
then ascend into the air to fly 30 feet more.
Being Prone:
Combatants often find themselves lying on the 
ground, either because they are knocked down or 
because they throw themselves down. In the game, 
they are prone, a condition described in appendix A.
You can drop prone without using any of your 
speed. Getting up takes more effort; doing so costs an 
amount of movement equal to half your speed. For 
example, if your speed is 30 feet, you must spend 15 
feet of movement to get up. You can’t get up if you 
don’t have enough movement left or if your speed is 0.
To move while prone, you must crawl or use magic 
such as teleportation. Every foot of movement while 
crawling costs 1 extra foot. Crawling 1 foot in 
difficult terrain, therefore, costs 3 feet of movement.
Interacting with Objects Around You
Here are a few examples of the sorts of thing you can do in 
tandem with your movement and action:
• draw or sheathe a sword
• open or close a door
• withdraw a potion from your backpack
• pick up a dropped axe
• take a bauble from a table
• remove a ring from your finger
• stuff some food into your mouth
• plant a banner in the ground
• fish a few coins from your belt pouch
• drink all the ale in a flagon
• throw a lever or a switch
• pull a torch from a sconce
• take a book from a shelf you can reach
• extinguish a small flame
• don a mask
• pull the hood of your cloak up and over your head
• put your ear to a door
• kick a small stone
• turn a key in a lock
• tap the floor with a 10-foot pole
• hand an item to another character
107
Moving Around Other
Flying Movement:
Flying creatures enjoy many benefits of mobility, but 
they must also deal with the danger of falling. If a 
flying creature is knocked prone, has its speed reduced 
to 0, or is otherwise deprived of the ability to move, 
the creature falls, unless it has the ability to hover or it 
is being held aloft by magic, such as by the fly spell.
Actions in Combat:
When you take your action on your turn, you can 
take one of the actions presented here, an action you 
gained from your steps or a special feature, or an 
action that you improvise. Many nonplayer creatures 
have action options of their own in their stat blocks.
When you describe an action not detailed elsewhere 
in the rules, the storyteller tells you whether that 
action is possible and what kind of roll you need to 
make, if any, to determine success or failure.
Cast a Spell:
Spellcaster characters, as well as many nonplayer 
creatures, have access to spells and can use them to 
great effect in combat. Each spell has a casting time, 
which specifies whether the caster must use an action, 
a reaction, minutes, or even hours to cast the spell. 
Casting a spell is, therefore, not necessarily an action. 
Most spells do have a casting time of 1 action, so a 
spellcaster often uses their action in combat to cast 
such a spell.
Dash:
When you take the Dash action, you gain extra 
movement for the current turn. The increase equals a 
number of 5-foot lengths equal to 2d4 + your Agility 
or Health (your choice), after applying any bonuses 
or penalties. With a speed of 30 feet, for example, you 
can move up to 60 feet on your turn if you dash and 
your roll totals 6.
Any increase or decrease to your speed changes this 
additional movement by the same amount. If your 
speed of 30 feet is reduced to 15 feet, for instance, you 
can move up to 30 feet this turn if you dash and your 
roll totals 6.
Dodge:
When you take the Dodge action, you focus entirely 
on avoiding attacks. Until the start of your next turn, 
you gain advantage on defense checks against any 
attack made against you, and you make Agility saving 
checks with advantage. You lose this benefit if you are 
incapacitated or if your speed drops to 0.
Help:
You can lend your aid to another creature in the 
completion of a task. When you take the Help action, 
the creature you aid gains advantage on the next 
ability check it makes to perform the task you are 
helping with, provided that it makes the check before 
the start of your next turn.
Alternatively, you can aid a friendly creature in 
attacking a creature within your reach. You feint, 
distract the target, or in some other way team up to 
make your ally’s attack more effective. If your ally 
attacks the target before your next turn, the first attack 
check is made with advantage.
Ready:
Sometimes you want to get the jump on a foe or wait 
for a particular circumstance before you act. To do so, 
you can take the Ready action on your turn, which 
lets you act using your reaction before the start of your 
next turn.
First, you decide what perceivable circumstance will 
trigger your reaction. Then, you choose the action you 
will take in response to that trigger, or you choose to 
move up to your speed in response to it. Examples 
include “If the cultist steps on the trapdoor, I’ll pull 
the lever that opens it,” and “If the goblin steps next 
to me, I move away.”
When the trigger occurs, you can either take your 
reaction right after the trigger finishes or ignore the 
trigger. Remember that you can take only one reaction 
per round.
When you ready a spell, you cast it as normal but 
hold its energy, which you release with your reaction 
when the trigger occurs. To be readied, a spell must 
have a casting time of 1 action, and holding onto 
the spell’s magic requires concentration. If your 
concentration is broken, the spell dissipates without 
taking effect. For example, if you are concentrating 
on the web spell and ready magic missile, your web 
spell ends, and if you suffer damage before you release 
magic missile with your reaction, your concentration 
might be broken.
Search:
When you take the Search action, you devote your 
attention to finding something. Depending on the 
nature of your search, the storyteller might have you 
make a Wisdom (Perception) check or an Intelligence 
(Investigation) check.
109
Use an Object:
You normally interact with an object while doing 
something else, such as when you draw a sword as part 
of an attack. When an object requires your action for 
its use, you take the Use an Object action. This action 
is also useful when you want to interact with more 
than one object on your turn.
Withdraw:
If you take the Withdraw action, your movement 
doesn’t provoke opportunity attacks for the rest of 
the turn.
Attack and Defense Checks:
You make an attack check whenever you take the 
Attack action; you make a defense check whenever 
you are the target of a nonplayer creature’s attack.
Attack Checks:
Some spells require the caster to roll an attack to 
determine whether the spell effect hits the intended 
target. Your attack bonus with a spell attack equals 
your spellcasting ability + your proficiency bonus.
Most spells that require attack checks involve 
ranged attacks. Remember that you have disadvantage 
on a ranged attack roll if you are within 5 feet of a 
hostile creature that can perceive you and that isn’t 
incapacitated.
Defense Checks:
When you are the target of an attack, you make a 
special kind of saving check called a defense check. To 
make a defense check, roll a d20 and add your defense 
bonus. The armor (and shield) you wear determines 
your defense bonus. If you aren’t wearing armor or 
wielding a shield, your defense bonus is equal to your 
Agility. If your defense check is successful, you avoid 
the attack’s damage. If your check fails, you suffer 
damage or the effect of the attack.
Rolling 1 or 20:
If the d20 roll for an attack or defense check is a 20, 
the check is successful regardless of any penalties or 
the Difficulty Score. A 20 on an attack roll is called a 
critical hit, which is explained later in this chapter.
If the d20 roll for an attack or defense check is a 1, 
the check is a failure regardless of any bonuses or the 
Difficulty Score.
Imperceptible Attackers and
Ranged Attacks:
When you make a ranged attack, you fire a bow or a 
crossbow, hurl a handaxe, or otherwise send projectiles 
to strike a foe at a distance. A nonplayer creature 
might shoot spines from its tail or some other natural 
ranged attack. Many spells also involve making a 
ranged attack.
Range:
The target of a spell must be within the spell’s range. 
For a spell like magic missile, the target is a creature. 
For a spell like fireball, the target is the point in space 
where the ball of fire erupts.
Most spells have ranges expressed in feet. Some 
spells can target only a creature (including you) that 
you touch. Other spells, such as the shield spell, affect 
only you. These spells have a range of self.
Spells that create cones or lines of effect that 
originate from you also have a range of self, indicating 
that the origin point of the spell’s effect must be you.
Once a spell is cast, its effects aren’t limited by its 
range, unless the spell’s description says otherwise.
Reach Attacks:
Used in hand-to-hand combat, a reach attack allows 
you to attack a foe within your reach. You can make 
a reach attack against an opponent you can pinpoint 
by sight, touch, echolocation, tremorsense, or a sixth 
sense. If you make the reach attack with another sense, 
you have disadvantage on the attack roll. A reach 
attack typically uses a handheld weapon such as a 
sword, a warhammer, or an axe. A typical nonplayer 
creature makes a reach attack when it strikes with its 
claws, horns, teeth, tentacles, or other body part. A 
few spells also involve making a reach attack.
Most creatures have a 5-foot reach and can thus 
attack targets within 5 feet of them when making a 
reach attack. Certain creatures (typically those larger 
than Medium) have reach attacks with a greater reach 
than 5 feet, as noted in their descriptions.
Instead of using a weapon to make a reach weapon 
attack, you can use an unarmed strike: a punch, 
kick, head-butt, or similar forceful blow (none of 
which count as weapons). On a hit, an unarmed 
strike inflicts bludgeoning damage equal to 1 + your 
Strength. You are proficient with your unarmed 
strikes.
Opportunity Attacks:
In a fight, everyone is constantly watching for a 
chance to strike an enemy who is fleeing or passing by. 
Such a strike is called an opportunity attack.
You can make an opportunity attack when a hostile 
creature that you can see moves out of your reach. To 
make the opportunity attack, you use your reaction to 
make one reach attack against the provoking creature. 
The attack occurs right before the creature leaves 
your reach.
You can avoid provoking an opportunity attack by 
taking the Withdraw action. You also don’t provoke 
an opportunity attack when you teleport or when 
someone or something moves you without using your 
movement, action, or reaction. For example, you don’t 
provoke an opportunity attack if an explosion hurls 
you out of a foe’s reach or if gravity causes you to fall 
past an enemy.
Two-Weapon Fighting:
When you take the Attack action and attack with a 
light reach weapon that you’re holding in one hand, 
you may also attack with a different light reach 
weapon that you’re holding in the other hand. If you 
have an ability bonus, don’t add it to the damage of 
the second attack.
If either weapon has the thrown property, you can 
throw the weapon, instead of making a reach attack 
with it.
Grab:
When you want to seize a creature or wrestle with 
it, you can use the Attack action to make a special 
reach attack, a grab. If you’re able to make multiple 
attacks with the Attack action, this attack replaces one 
of them.
The target of your grab must be no more than one 
size larger than you and must be within your reach. 
Using at least one free hand, you try to seize the target 
by making a grab check instead of an attack check: 
a Strength (Athletics) check contested by the target’s 
Contests in Combat
Battle often involves pitting your prowess against that of your 
foe. Such a challenge is represented by a contest. This section 
includes the most common contests that require an action in 
combat: grabbing and shoving a creature. The storyteller can use 
these contests as models for improvising others.
111
Strength (Athletics) or Agility (Acrobatics) check 
(the target chooses the ability to use). If you succeed, 
you subject the target to the seized condition. The 
condition specifies the things that end it, and you 
can release the target whenever you like (no action 
required).
You can use your action to try to pin a creature 
seized by your ally. To do so, make a grab check. If 
you succeed, you, your ally, and the target are all 
restrained until the pin ends by the pinned creature 
escaping at least one grab.
Escaping a Grab. A seized creature can use its 
action to escape. To do so, it must succeed on a 
Strength (Athletics) or Agility (Acrobatics) check 
contested by your Strength (Athletics) check.
Moving a Seized Creature. When you move, you 
can drag or carry the seized creature with you, but 
your speed is halved, unless the creature is two or 
more sizes smaller than you. A pinned creature can 
only be moved if the creatures pinning it both expend 
their movement.
Shoving a Creature:
Using the Attack action, you can make a special reach 
attack to shove a creature, either to knock it prone or 
push it away from you. If you’re able to make multiple 
attacks with the Attack action, this attack replaces one 
of them.
The target must be no more than one size larger 
than you and must be within your reach. Instead 
of making an attack check, you make a Strength 
(Athletics) check contested by the target’s Strength 
(Athletics) or Agility (Acrobatics) check (the target 
chooses the ability to use). If you win the contest, you 
either knock the target prone or push it 5 feet away 
from you.
Damage and Healing:
Injury and the risk of death are constant companions 
of those who explore fantasy worlds. The thrust of a 
sword, a well-placed arrow, or a blast of flame from a 
fireball spell all have the potential to damage, or even 
kill, the hardiest of creatures.
Damage Rolls:
Each weapon, spell, and harmful nonplayer creature 
ability specifies the damage it inflicts. You roll the 
damage die or dice, add any bonuses or penalties, 
and apply the damage to your target. Magic weapons, 
special abilities, and other factors can grant a bonus 
to damage. With a penalty, it is possible to inflict 0 
damage, but never negative damage.
When attacking with a weapon, you add your 
ability—the same number used for the attack check—
to the damage. A spell tells you which dice to roll for 
damage and whether to add any bonuses or penalties. 
If a spell or other effect inflicts damage to more than 
one target at the same time, roll the damage once 
for all of them. For example, when a character casts 
fireball or flame strike, the spell’s damage is rolled once 
for all creatures caught in the blast.
Critical Hit:
When you score a critical hit, you get to roll extra 
dice for the attack’s damage against the target. 
Nonplayer creatures score a critical hit when a player 
rolls a 1 on their defense check. Roll all of the attack’s 
damage dice twice and add them together. Then add 
any relevant bonuses or penalties as normal. To speed 
up play, you can roll all the damage dice 
at once.
For example, if you score a critical hit with a 
dagger, roll 2d4 for the damage, rather than 1d4, and 
then add your relevant ability. If the attack involves 
other damage dice, such as from the Sneaky step 
feature, you roll those dice twice as well.
Damage Types:
Different attacks, damaging spells, and other harmful 
effects inflict different types of damage. Damage types 
have no rules of their own, but other rules, such as 
damage resistance, rely on the types.
The damage types follow, with examples to help a 
storyteller assign a damage type to a new effect.
Acid. The corrosive spray of acid breath and the 
dissolving enzymes secreted by an ooze inflict acid 
damage.
Bludgeoning. Blunt force attacks—hammers, 
falling, constriction, and the like—inflict bludgeoning 
damage.
Cold. The biting winds and snow of a blizzard inflict 
cold damage.
Fire. Magma, heat waves, an open flame, and many 
spells inflict fire damage.
Force. Force is pure magical energy focused into a 
harmful form. Most effects that inflict force damage 
are spells.
Lightning. A bolt of lightning and the current of an 
electric eel both inflict lightning damage.
Necrotic. Necrotic damage, inflicted by certain 
undead or spells, withers matter and even the soul.
Piercing. Puncturing and impaling attacks, 
including spears and bites, inflict piercing damage.
Poison. Venomous stings and toxic gas inflict 
poison damage.
Psychic. Mental abilities, such as a psionic blast, 
inflict psychic damage.
Radiant. Radiant damage, inflicted by a flame strike 
spell or a holy smiting weapon, sears the flesh like fire 
and overloads the spirit with power.
Slashing. Swords, axes, and claws inflict slashing 
damage.
Thunder. A concussive burst of sound, such as 
the effect of the thunderwave spell, inflicts thunder 
damage.
Damage Resistance and 
Vulnerability
Some creatures and objects are exceedingly difficult or 
unusually easy to hurt with certain types of damage.
If a creature or an object has resistance to a damage 
type, damage of that type is halved against it. If a 
creature or an object has vulnerability to a damage 
type, damage of that type is doubled against it.
Resistance and then vulnerability are applied 
after all other bonuses and penalties to damage. For 
example, a creature has resistance to bludgeoning 
damage and is hit by an attack that inflicts 25 
bludgeoning damage. The creature is also within a 
magical aura that reduces all damage by 5. The 25 
damage is first reduced by 5 and then halved, so the 
creature suffers 10 damage.
Multiple instances of resistance or vulnerability 
that affect the same damage type count as only one 
instance. For example, if a creature has resistance to fire 
damage as well as resistance to all nonmagical damage, 
the damage of a nonmagical fire is reduced by half 
against the creature, not reduced by three-quarters.
113
Empty Health Pool:
When your health pool is emptied, you either die 
outright or fall unconscious, as explained in the 
following sections.
Instant Death. Massive damage can kill you 
instantly. When damage empties your health pool and 
there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining 
damage equals or exceeds your health pool’s depth.
For example, a character whose health pool’s 
depth is 12 currently has 6 drops in her health 
pool. If she suffers 18 damage from an attack, she is 
reduced to 0, but 12 damage remains. Because the 
remaining damage equals her health pool’s depth, the 
character dies.
Falling Unconscious. If damage empties your 
health pool but fails to kill you, you fall unconscious. 
This unconsciousness ends if your health pool is 
replenished by even 1 drop.
Death Rolls. Whenever you start your turn with 
an empty health pool, you must make a special saving 
check, called a death roll, to determine whether you 
creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other 
saving checks, this one isn’t tied to any ability. You 
are in the hands of fate now, aided only by spells and 
features that improve your chances of succeeding on a 
saving check.
Roll a d20. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. 
Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect 
by itself. On your third success, you become stable 
(see below). On your third failure, you die. The 
successes and failures don’t need to be consecutive; 
keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. 
The number of both is reset to zero when you regain 
any health or become stable.
When you make a death roll and roll a 1 on the 
d20, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the 
d20, you replenish 1 drop to your health pool.
Damage on Empty. If you suffer any damage while 
you have an empty health pool, you suffer a death roll 
failure. If the damage is from a critical hit, you suffer 
two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds 
your health pool depth, you suffer instant death.
Stabilizing a Creature. The best way to save a 
creature with an empty health pool is to heal it. If 
healing is unavailable, the creature can at least be 
stabilized so that it isn’t killed by a failed death roll.
You can use your action to administer first aid 
to an unconscious creature and attempt to stabilize 
it, which requires a successful DS 10 Intelligence 
(Medicine) check.
A stable creature doesn’t make death rolls, even 
though it has an empty health pool, but it does remain 
unconscious. The creature stops being stable, and must 
start making death rolls again, if it suffers any damage. 
A stable creature that isn’t healed replenishes 1 drop to 
its health pool after 1d4 hours.
Nonplayer Creatures 
and Death
Storytellers can have a nonplayer creature die the 
instant its health pool is emptied, rather than having 
it fall unconscious and make death rolls. Mighty 
villains and special nonplayer creatures are common 
exceptions; the storyteller might have them fall 
unconscious and follow the same rules as characters.
Knocking Out a Creature:
Sometimes an attacker wants to incapacitate a foe, 
rather than inflict a killing blow. When an attacker 
empties a creature’s health pool with a reach attack, 
the attacker can knock the creature out. The attacker 
can make this choice the instant the damage is 
inflicted. The creature falls unconscious and is stable.
Second Health Pools:
Some spells and special abilities confer a second 
health pool to a creature. A second health pool is a 
separate pool that serves as a buffer against damage, 
protecting you from injury.
When you have a second health pool and suffer 
damage, the second health pool is emptied first, and 
any leftover damage carries over to your normal health 
pool. For example, if you have 5 drops in your second
Mounted Combat:
A knight charging into battle on a warhorse, a mage 
casting spells from the back of a griffon, or a priest 
soaring through the sky on a pegasus all enjoy the 
benefits of speed and mobility that a mount can 
provide.
A willing creature that is at least one size larger than 
you and that has an appropriate anatomy can serve as 
a mount, using the following rules.
Mounting and Dismounting:
Once during your move, you can mount a creature 
that is within 5 feet of you or dismount. Doing so 
costs an amount of movement equal to half your 
speed. For example, if your speed is 30 feet, you 
must spend 15 feet of movement to mount a horse. 
Therefore, you can’t mount it if you don’t have 15 feet 
of movement left or if your speed is 0.
If an effect moves your mount against its will while 
you’re on it, you must succeed on a DS 10 Agility 
saving check or fall off the mount, landing prone in a 
space within 5 feet of it. If you’re knocked prone while 
mounted, you must make the same saving check.
If your mount is knocked prone, you can use your 
reaction to dismount it as it falls and land on your 
feet. Otherwise, you are dismounted and fall prone in 
a space within 5 feet of it.
Controlling a Mount:
While you’re mounted, you have two options. You 
can either control the mount or allow it to act 
independently. Intelligent creatures, such as dragons, 
act independently.
You can control a mount only if it has been trained 
to accept a rider. Domesticated horses, donkeys, and 
similar creatures are assumed to have such training. 
While in combat, the turn order of a controlled 
mount changes to match yours when you mount it. 
It moves as you direct it, and it has only three action 
options: Dash, Dodge, and Withdraw. A controlled 
mount can move and act even on the turn that you 
mount it.
An independent mount retains its place in turn 
order. Bearing a rider puts no restrictions on the 
actions the mount can take, and it moves and acts as it 
wishes. It might flee from combat, rush to attack and 
devour a badly injured foe, or otherwise act against 
your wishes.
In either case, if the mount provokes an opportunity 
attack while you’re on it, the attacker can target you or 
the mount.
Underwater Combat:
When adventurers pursue merfolk back to their 
undersea homes, fight off sharks in an ancient 
shipwreck, or find themselves in a villain’s flooded lair, 
they must fight in a challenging environment. While 
underwater, the following rules apply.
When making a reach weapon attack, a creature 
that doesn’t have a swimming speed (either natural 
or granted by magic) has disadvantage on the 
attack check unless the weapon is a dagger, javelin, 
shortsword, spear, or trident.
A ranged weapon attack automatically misses a 
target beyond the weapon’s normal range. Even against 
a target within normal range, the attack check has 
disadvantage unless the weapon is a crossbow, a net, 
or a weapon that is thrown like a javelin (including a 
spear, trident, or dart).
Creatures and objects that are fully immersed in 
water have resistance to fire damage.

What Is a Spell?:
A spell is a discrete magical effect, a single shaping of 
the magical energies that suffuse the multiverse into 
a specific, limited expression. Spells can be versatile 
tools, weapons, or protective wards. They can inflict 
damage or undo it, impose or remove conditions, 
drain life energy away, and restore life to the dead.
Uncounted thousands of spells have been created 
over the course of the multiverse’s history, and many 
of them are long forgotten. Some might yet lie 
recorded in crumbling spellbooks hidden in ancient 
ruins or trapped in the minds of dead gods. Or they 
might someday be reinvented by a character who has 
amassed enough power and wisdom to do so.

Known Spells:
Before a spellcaster can use a spell, he or she must 
have the spell firmly fixed in mind, or must have 
access to the spell in a magic item. Spellcasters have a 
limited list of spells they know that are always fixed in 
mind. Other spellcasters cast spells from an heirloom 
or magic item. This process varies for different 
characters, as detailed in their features.
In every case, the number of spells a caster can 
have fixed in mind at any given time depends on the 
character’s step features.
Spell Slots:
Regardless of how many spells a caster knows, they 
can cast only a limited number of spells before resting. 
Manipulating the fabric of magic and channeling 
its energy into even a simple spell is physically and 
mentally taxing, and higher-level spells are even more 
so. Thus, each spellcasting character’s step features 
detail how many spell slots of each spell level a 
character can use.
Finishing a long rest restores any expended spell 
slots. Some creatures have special abilities that let 
them cast spells without using spell slots.
Casting a Spell at a Higher Level:
When a spellcaster casts a spell using a slot that is of a 
higher level than the spell, the spell assumes the higher 
level for that casting. For instance, if Umara casts 
magic missile using one of her 2nd-level slots, that 
magic missile is 2nd level. Effectively, the spell expands 
to fill the slot it is put into.
Some spells, such as magic missile and cure wounds, 
have more powerful effects when cast at a higher level, 
as detailed in a spell’s description.

Those Who Wander is a dynamic fantasy tabletop game system 
distinct for its exponentially growing character paths, diverse and versatile 
parentages, enigmatic and awakening heirlooms, mechanically defining 
character backgrounds, and more.
The game epitomizes the journey made of numberless steps. Each step is a 
decision— left or right. And each decision leaves its mark on you. No matter 
where you wander, we hope you feel at home all along the way.
Rituals:
Certain spells have a special tag: ritual. Such a spell 
can be cast following the normal rules for spellcasting, 
or the spell can be cast as a ritual. The ritual version of 
a spell takes 10 minutes longer to cast than normal. It 
also doesn’t expend a spell slot, which means the ritual 
version of a spell can’t be cast at a higher level.
To cast a spell as a ritual, the caster must have the 
spell among their known spells.
Casting in Armor
Because of the mental focus and precise gestures required for 
spellcasting, you must be proficient with the armor you are 
wearing to cast a spell. You are otherwise too distracted and 
physically hampered by your armor for spellcasting.

Casting Time:
Most spells require a single action to cast, but some 
spells require only a reaction or much more time 
to cast.
Longer Casting Times:
Certain spells (including spells cast as rituals) require 
more time to cast: minutes or even hours. When you 
cast a spell with a casting time longer than a single 
action or reaction, you must spend your action each 
turn casting the spell, and you must maintain your 
concentration while you do so. If your concentration 
is broken, the spell fails, but you don’t expend a spell 
slot. If you want to try casting the spell again, you 
must start over.
Components:
A spell’s components are the physical requirements 
you must meet in order to cast it. Each spell’s 
description indicates whether it requires articulated 
(A), somatic (S), or material (M) components. If you 
can’t provide one or more of a spell’s components, you 
are unable to cast the spell.
Articulated (A):
Most spells require the utterance, signing, or visual 
vernacular of mystic phrases. The words themselves 
aren’t the source of the spell’s power; rather, the 
particular combination of sounds or signs sets the 
threads of magic in motion. A character who is 
gagged or in an area of silence, such as one created by 
the silence spell, can’t cast a spell with an articulated 
component, unless they are fluent in at least one sign 
language. A character who does not have free use of 
at least one hand can’t cast a spell with an articulated 
component, unless they can vocalize it or use visual 
vernacular.
Somatic (S):
Spellcasting gestures might include a forceful 
gesticulation or an intricate set of gestures. This is 
in addition to any articulated component, whether 
vocalized or signed, if the spell requires both. If a spell 
requires a somatic component, the caster must have 
free use of at least one hand to perform these gestures.
Material (M):
Casting some spells requires particular objects, 
specified in parentheses in the component entry. 
A character can use an heirloom, component pouch, 
or spellcasting focus (found in “Equipment”) in 
place of the components specified for a spell. But if a 
cost is indicated for a component, a character must 
have that specific component before he or she can cast 
the spell.
If a spell states that a material component is 
consumed by the spell, the caster must provide this 
component for each casting of the spell.
A spellcaster must have a hand free to access a 
spell’s material components—or to hold a spellcasting 
focus—but it can be the same hand that he or she uses 
to perform somatic components.

Instantaneous:
Many spells are instantaneous. The spell harms, heals, 
creates, or alters a creature or an object in a way that 
can’t be dispelled, because its magic exists only for an 
instant.
Concentration:
Some spells require you to maintain concentration 
in order to keep their magic active. If you lose 
concentration, such a spell ends.
If a spell must be maintained with concentration, 
that fact appears in its Duration entry, and the spell 
specifies how long you can concentrate on it. You can 
end concentration at any time (no action required).
Normal activity, such as moving and attacking, 
doesn’t interfere with concentration. The following 
factors can break concentration:
• Casting another spell that requires
concentration. You lose concentration on a spell if
you cast another spell that requires concentration.
You can’t concentrate on two spells at once.
• Suffering damage. Whenever you suffer damage
while you are concentrating on a spell, you must
make a Health saving check to maintain your
concentration. The DS equals 10 or half the
damage you take, whichever number is higher. If
you take damage from multiple sources, such as an
arrow and a dragon’s breath, you make a separate
saving check for each source of damage.
• Being incapacitated or killed. You lose
concentration on a spell if you are incapacitated or
if you die.
The storyteller might also decide that certain
environmental phenomena, such as a wave crashing 
over you while you’re on a storm-tossed ship, require 
you to succeed on a DS 10 Health saving check to 
maintain concentration on a spell.
A Clear Path to the Target:
To target something, you must have a clear path to it, 
so it can’t be behind total cover.
If you place an area of effect at a specific point and 
an obstruction, such as a wall, is between you and that 
point, the point of origin comes into being on the 
near side of that obstruction.
Targeting Yourself:
If a spell targets a creature of your choice, you can 
choose yourself, unless the creature must be hostile 
or specifically a creature other than you. If you are 
in the area of effect of a spell you cast, you can target 
yourself.
Areas of Effect:
Spells such as burning hands and cone of cold cover 
an area, allowing them to affect multiple creatures 
at once.
A spell’s description specifies its area of effect, which 
typically has one of five different shapes: cone, cube, 
cylinder, line, or sphere. Every area of effect has a 
point of origin, a location from which the spell’s 
energy erupts. The rules for each shape specify how 
you position its point of origin. Typically, a point of 
origin is a point in space, but some spells have an area 
whose origin is a creature or an object.
A spell’s effect expands in straight lines from the 
point of origin. If no unblocked straight line extends 
from the point of origin to a location within the area 
of effect, that location isn’t included in the spell’s area. 
To block one of these imaginary lines, an obstruction 
must provide total cover.
Cone:
A cone extends in a direction you choose from its 
point of origin. A cone’s width at a given point along 
its length is equal to that point’s distance from the 
point of origin. A cone’s area of effect specifies its 
maximum length.
A cone’s point of origin is not included in the cone’s 
area of effect, unless you decide otherwise.
Cube:
You select a cube’s point of origin, which lies 
anywhere on a face of the cubic effect. The cube’s size 
is expressed as the length of each side.
A cube’s point of origin is not included in the cube’s 
area of effect, unless you decide otherwise.
Cylinder:
A cylinder’s point of origin is the center of a circle of a 
particular radius, as given in the spell description. The 
circle must either be on the ground or at the height 
of the spell effect. The energy in a cylinder expands in 
straight lines from the point of origin to the perimeter 
of the circle, forming the base of the cylinder. The 
spell’s effect then shoots up from the base or down 
from the top, to a distance equal to the height of the 
cylinder.
A cylinder’s point of origin is included in the 
cylinder’s area of effect.
Line:
A line extends from its point of origin in a straight 
path up to its length and covers an area defined by 
its width.
A line’s point of origin is not included in the line’s 
area of effect, unless you decide otherwise.
Sphere:
You select a sphere’s point of origin, and the sphere 
extends outward from that point. The sphere’s size 
is expressed as a radius in feet that extends from 
the point.
A sphere’s point of origin is included in the sphere’s 
area of effect.
Combining Magical Effects:
The effects of different spells add together while the 
durations of those spells overlap. The effects of the 
same spell cast multiple times don’t combine, however. 
Instead, the most potent effect—such as the highest 
bonus—from those castings applies while their 
durations overlap.
For example, if two priests cast bless on the same 
target, that character gains the spell’s benefit only 
once; they don’t get to roll two bonus dice.
The Schools of Magic
Academies of magic group spells into eight categories called 
schools of magic. Scholars, particularly mages, apply these 
categories to all spells, believing that all magic functions in 
essentially the same way, whether it derives from rigorous study 
or is bestowed by a deity.
The schools of magic help describe spells; they have no rules 
of their own, although some rules refer to the schools.
Abjuration spells are protective in nature, though some of 
them have aggressive uses. They create magical barriers, negate 
harmful effects, harm trespassers, or banish creatures to other 
planes of existence.
Conjuration spells involve the transportation of objects and 
creatures from one location to another. Some spells summon 
creatures or objects to the caster’s side, whereas others allow 
the caster to teleport to another location. Some conjurations 
create objects or effects out of nothing.
Divination spells reveal information, whether in the form of 
secrets long forgotten, glimpses of the future, the locations of 
hidden things, the truth behind illusions, or visions of distant 
people or places.
Enchantment spells affect the minds of others, influencing 
their behavior. Such spells can make enemies reconsider how 
they feel about the caster, tempt creatures to take a course of 
action, or even leave creatures in a euphoric haze.
Evocation spells manipulate magical energy to produce a 
desired effect. Some call up blasts of fire or lightning. Others 
channel positive energy to heal wounds.
Illusion spells deceive the senses or minds of others. They 
cause people to see things that are not there, to miss things that 
are there, to hear phantom noises, or to remember things that 
never happened. Some illusions create phantom images that any 
creature can see, but the most insidious illusions plant an image 
directly in the mind of a creature.
Necromancy spells manipulate the energies of life and death. 
Such spells can grant an extra reserve of life force, drain the life 
energy from another creature, create the undead, or even bring 
the dead back to life.
Transmutation spells change the properties of a creature, 
object, or environment. They might turn an enemy into a 
harmless creature, bolster the strength of an ally, make an object 
move at the caster’s command, or enhance a creature’s innate 
healing abilities to rapidly recover from injury.

Appendix B: Conditions
C
onditions alter a creature’s 
capabilities in a variety of ways 
and can arise as a result of a spell, 
a feature, a creature’s attack, or 
other effect. Most conditions, such 
as disoriented, are impairments, 
but a few, such as invisible, can be 
advantageous.
A condition lasts either until it is countered (the 
prone condition is countered by getting up, for 
example) or for a duration specified by the effect that 
imposed the condition.
If multiple effects impose the same condition on a 
creature, each instance of the condition has its own 
duration, but the condition’s effects don’t get worse. A 
creature either has a condition or doesn’t.
The following definitions specify what happens to a 
creature while it is subjected to a condition.
dISorIented
• A disoriented creature automatically doesn’t succeed
any ability check that requires its primary senses.
• Attack checks against the creature have advantage,
and the creature’s attack checks have disadvantage.
Enraptured
• An enraptured creature can’t attack any creature or
target it with harmful abilities or magical effects.
• Attempts to interact socially with the enraptured
creature have disadvantage on the ability check.
Exhaustion
Some special abilities and environmental hazards, such 
as starvation and the long-term effects of freezing or 
scorching temperatures, can lead to a special condition 
called exhaustion. Exhaustion is measured in six levels. 
An effect can give a creature one or more levels of 
exhaustion, as specified in the effect's description.

If an already exhausted creature suffers another 
effect that causes exhaustion, its current level of

A creature suffers the effect of its current level of

An effect that removes exhaustion reduces its level as

Finishing a long rest reduces a creature’s exhaustion

Frightened
• A frightened creature has disadvantage on ability
checks and attack checks while the source of its fear
is within line of sight or earshot.
• The creature can’t willingly move closer to the
source of its fear.
Incapacitated
• An incapacitated creature can’t take actions or
reactions.
Inert
• An inert creature is incapacitated (see the
condition) and can't move, speak, or sign.
• The creature automatically fails Strength and Agility
saving checks.
• Attack checks against the creature have advantage.
• Any attack that hits the creature is a critical hit if
the attacker is within 5 feet of the creature.
Invisible
• An invisible creature is impossible to perceive
without the aid of magic or a sense other than
sight. For the purpose of hiding, the creature is
heavily obscured. The creature’s location can be
detected by any noise it makes or any tracks it
leaves.
• Attack rolls made by a sighted attacker against the
creature have disadvantage, and the creature’s attack
rolls against sighted targets have advantage.
Petrified
• A petrified creature is transformed, along with any
nonmagical object it is wearing or carrying, into a
solid inanimate substance (usually stone). Its weight
increases by a factor of ten, and it ceases aging.

Telepathy:
Telepathy is a magical ability that allows a creature to 
communicate mentally with another creature within 
a specified range. The contacted creature doesn’t need 
to share a language with the creature to communicate 
in this way with it, but it must be able to understand 
at least one language. A creature without telepathy can 
receive and respond to telepathic messages but can’t 
initiate or terminate a telepathic conversation.
A telepathic creature doesn’t need to perceive a 
contacted creature and can end the telepathic contact 
at any time. The contact is broken as soon as the two 
creatures are no longer within range of each other or 
if the telepathic creature contacts a different creature 
within range. A telepathic creature can initiate or 
terminate a telepathic conversation without using 
an action, but if the creature is incapacitated, it can’t 
initiate telepathic contact, and any current contact is 
terminated.
A creature within the area of an antimagic field or in 
any other location where magic doesn’t function can’t 
send or receive telepathic messages.
Experience Points:
The number of experience points (XP) a monster 
is worth is based on its challenge score. Experience 
points are awarded for defeating the creature or by 
neutralizing the threat posed by the creature through 
trickery, diplomacy, or nonviolent contest.
Unless something tells you otherwise, a creature 
summoned by a spell or other magical ability is worth 
the XP noted in its stat block.
Special Traits:
Special traits (which appear after a creature’s 
challenge score but before any actions or reactions) 
are characteristics that are likely to be relevant in a 
combat encounter and that require some explanation.
Innate Spellcasting:
A creature with the innate ability to cast spells has 
the Innate Spellcasting special trait. Unless noted 
otherwise, an innate spell of 1st level or higher is 
always cast at its lowest possible level and can’t be cast 
at a higher level. If a creature has a cantrip where its 
level matters and no level is given, use the creature’s 
challenge score.
An innate spell can have special rules or restrictions. 
For example, a creature might be able to innately 
cast the levitate spell, but the spell has a “self only” 
restriction, which means that the spell affects only the 
spellcaster.
A creature’s innate spells can’t be swapped out with 
other spells. If a creature’s innate spells don’t require 
attack rolls, no attack bonus is given for them.
Reach and Ranged Attacks:
Two actions that a creature can take in combat are 
reach and ranged attacks. These can be spell attacks 
or weapon attacks, where the “weapon” might be a 
manufactured item or a natural weapon, such as a 
claw or tail spike. For more information on different 
kinds of attacks, see the “Playing the Game” chapter.
Creature vs. Target. The target of a reach or ranged 
attack is usually either one creature or one target, the 
difference being that a “target” can be a creature or an 
object.
Hit. Any damage inflicted or other effects that occur 
as a result of an attack hitting a target are described 
after the “Hit” notation. You have the option of 
inflicting average damage or rolling the damage; for 
this reason, both the average damage and the die 
expression are presented.
Miss. If an attack has an effect that occurs on a 
miss, that information is presented after the “Miss” 
notation.
Multiattack:
A creature that can make multiple attacks on its 
turn has the Multiattack action. A creature can’t use 
Multiattack when making an opportunity attack, 
which must be a single reach attack.
Limited Usage:
Some special abilities have restrictions on the number 
of times they can be used.
X/Day. The notation “X/Day” means a special 
ability can be used X number of times and that a 
creature must finish a long rest to regain expended 
uses. For example, “1/Day” means a special ability can 
be used once and that the creature must finish a long 
rest to use it again.
Recharge X–Y. The notation “Recharge X–Y” means 
that a creature can use a special ability once and that 
the ability then has a random chance of recharging 
during each subsequent round of combat. At the 
start of each of the creature’s turns, roll a d6. If the 
roll is one of the numbers in the recharge notation, 
the creature regains the use of the special ability. The 
ability also recharges when the creature finishes a short 
or long rest.
For example, “Recharge 5–6” means a creature can 
use the special ability once. Then, at the start of the 
creature’s turn, it regains the use of that ability if it 
rolls a 5 or 6 on a d6.
Recharge after a Short or Long Rest. This 
notation means that a creature can use a special ability 
once and then must finish a short or long rest to use it 
again.

Angels:
Often depicted as exquisite humanoids with luminous 
wings, angels are celestial creatures that act as the 
hands and feet of deities. Created by gods, these 
legendary celestials enact the will of the deity they 
serve, whether as messengers, soldiers, or arbiters. 
While they are traditional natives to higher planes, 
they can be found in whatever realm a god has made 
their domain. 
Most angels are moral champions, made by 
deities who embody respectable ideals, for wicked 
and malevolent gods prefer more fiendish servitors. 
However, angels are not beholden to goodness, and 
those that choose another path are often considered 
“fallen” by others. Those that embrace evil pursuits 
often reflect it in their appearance, such as with dark 
wings. 
In addition, while angels are typically seen in a 
humanoid appearance, they are rumored to have 
another form that is far more incognizable to mortal 
perceptions. As to not disturb mortal sensibilities, they 
often prefer a more humanoid appearance for such 
affairs unless their duty involves striking such terror.
Cherubs
With two pairs of wings, cherubs occupy the middle 
of the hierarchy of angels. These celestials are often 
tasked by their gods with assignments in other planes 
that are too dangerous for a deva to complete or hold 
the rank of captains in celestial armies.

Animated Objects:
Oftentimes, powerful spellcasters such as archmages 
or mighty sorcerers enchant mundane objects with 
incredible arcane power to animate them. These 
animated objects are most often used as guardians 
to protect the spellcaster’s domain or secrets, but a 
creative individual could find other uses for them 
as well.
While not typical, some spellcasters are so strong 
that they can imbue animated objects with sentience. 
Other times, an animated object naturally develops 
sentience if it has been animated by magic for decades 
or longer.
Animated Armor
For a reclusive archmage deep in study, armored 
guards need not only lodging, but pay, and can be 
quite the distraction. Hence, animating a suit of 
armor is a simple way to have loyal guards that need 
very little maintenance and do not interrupt any work. 
Relentless defenders, animated armors protect what 
they have been assigned to with unyielding dedication 
until they are too damaged to move or until the 
enchantment that animates them is unraveled.

Ankhegs:
These enormous insectoid monsters are natively found 
throughout the Material Planes in nearly every biome 
aside from the most inhospitable. Scholars note that 
ankheg colonies seem to act as a unified entity, with 
their societies drawing parallels to people’s civilizations 
in the way they divide labor, communicate with each 
other, and solve complex problems.
While ankhegs are not necessarily aggressive if left 
alone, their colonies can often grow near people’s 
settlements, where they can exploit nearby resources 
for the sake of expanding and developing their 
homes, and defend themselves if they feel threatened. 
Oftentimes, this can lead to conflict with nearby 
towns and cities.

Apes:
These tailless primates are native to forests, especially 
rainforests, and include specific beasts such as 
orangutans, gorillas, and chimpanzees. They are 
omnivores, but lean mostly toward eating plants. 
Exposure to magic and other environmental factors 
can contribute to a subspecies of giant apes. While 
fairly territorial, careful travelers can avoid hostility 
if they are careful and respectful while within a giant 
ape’s territory.

bats eat insects, fruit, or nectar. However, some bats 
feed on blood, and thus have associated the species 
as a whole with vampires. While giant bats are not as 
dangerous as they look, they are often hunted out of 
fear that they could be a vampire.

meadows, and along coasts. While black and brown 
bears are omnivores, polar bears are carnivorous and 
are found in arctic regions.

Centaurs:
Most centaurs assume they are the bastard children 
of some nature god. Many believe they are the 
creation of an elven nature spirit that bore them from 
the ground to protect nature. But because of the 
uncertainty of their origins they don’t worship any god 
or spirit for fear of angering the one that made them.
The People
Centaurs seem half person, half horse. Their person 
half can look as varied as any other people. 
They form semi-nomadic groups that travel in large 
herds across grasslands. The herd size fluctuates, as 
different clans may join or leave at any given moment. 
They stand as defenders of the land, nurturing injured 
creatures and fending off people who would destroy 
their natural habitat. They have excellent relations 
with people of any ancestry who are dedicated to 
preserving the land. They can be fierce allies or 
hated foes.

Demons:
There are a multitude of fates for a person’s soul at 
the time of their death. For those of particular infamy 
and evil, one of those fates is being cast into the 
lower planes and into the hands of fiends. Of the two 
kinds of fiends that hold dominion over the nether 
realms, demons are jailers, overseers, and soldiers—
ensuring that the souls they hold remain to receive the 
punishment they deserve by preventing escape and 
stopping incursions from would-be rescuers.
Should a strong soul declare intent to improve 
themselves from their mortal nature, they may have 
the opportunity to become an intelligent demon if 
they are judged to have bettered themselves.
However, after a lifetime spent in eternal service 
watching over the worst of people, there are plenty of 
demons who are dissatisfied with their charge. Some 
are motivated to find their own way, but others seek to 
destroy the worlds that would produce such despicable 
souls. 
Balor
The mightiest of demons, balors are enormous 
horned giants with massive bat-like wings. They are 
infused with sulphurous power, which grants them 
preternatural might, but is unleashed in an inferno 
upon their demise. Balors are typically generals of 
demon armies, the wardens over entire cell blocks of 
souls, or the guards for the very worst souls the depths 
contain. Those very same souls are usually the ones 
with the will to become balors themselves, but such 
souls have the greatest hurdle to overcome: pride.

Dinosaurs:
Diverse and magnificent reptiles, dinosaurs are 
primordial beasts that roamed the planes since they 
were still new. They dwelt within the seas, dominated 
the lands, and mastered the skies, and were as likely to 
be apex predators as they were to be migratory grazers. 
Many cultures reference dinosaurs in myths and 
legends, and ancient craftsmanship often depicts their 
mighty forms in varied interpretations.
It is commonly considered that dinosaurs were 
victims of historical calamities that shaped the 
multiverse. However, in the wildest reaches of the 
world it is rumored that some of them yet survive, 
sovereigns of a land that is untouched by the ravages 
of time. 
Plesiosaurus
The plesiosaurus is a carnivorous predator that dwells 
in marine habitats. They are agile swimmers propelled 
by two sets of fins on a turtle-shaped torso, and have 
a neck nearly the length of their body. Plesiosaurus 
are smaller than many of their terrestrial cousins and 
also differ by giving live birth rather than their young 
hatching from eggs. Due to water routes, some claim 
to have seen plesiosaurus in waters closer to people’s 
lands—though some even swear they have seen them 
in entirely closed lakes.

Dogs:
Domesticated from wild wolves, dogs are carnivorous 
canines that throughout history have been reliable 
companions for people of all lands. Bred throughout 
the ages into many different subspecies, dogs come 
in incredibly diverse shapes, sizes, and colorations. 
Depending on their owner, they can be hunters, 
helpers, laborers, defenders, or simply companions. 
A well-treated dog is loyal to its owner and comes to 
their aid for almost anything. Given the prominence 
of dogs and their notable attributes, it is unsurprising 
to find creatures of other natures that resemble them 
and are given their name—such as blink dogs and 
death dogs.
Blink Dog
A blink dog takes its name from its ability to blink 
in and out of existence, a talent it uses to facilitate 
its attacks and to avoid harm. These fey spirits are 
thought to have taken on an appearance resembling 
canines in order to foster a relationship with other fey 
that mimics the bond between people and their dogs. 
Blink dogs are exceptionally loyal to other fey and to 
each other, and fervently defend the territory of their 
companions.

Doppelganger:
Doppelgangers were spawned fully formed from the 
mind of Dreja, the Mother of all Monsters. With 
just one overwhelming drive—spreading chaos—
doppelgangers went out into the world to fulfill the 
instinct. 
the people
Doppelgangers in their natural form appear as tall and 
slender gray-skinned, hairless beings. They lack any 
apparent sex characteristics and have milky white eyes. 
Since they spend most of their time infiltrating 
other lineages, they mostly have no culture of their 
own. They are able to sense each other when using 
their mind-reading ability without any sort of 
detection.
Occasionally when a doppelganger has deemed 
they’ve sowed enough chaos in the world, they settle 
down somewhere and live life the best way they know 
how, sometimes as a complete new identity, sometimes 
taking on the identity of someone they’ve shapeshifted 
into. When this happens, other doppelgangers tend 
to be drawn to them, at least for a time, before 
going back out into the world. Other times, a weary 
doppelganger tries to find the Mother of all Monsters 
and have her absorb them back into her.

Dragons:
Dragons are intelligent, winged reptilians of ancient 
origin. A standout characteristic is their ability to 
breathe fire or other destructive energy, laying waste to 
entire armies of those who dare oppose them. Dragons 
can live hundreds of years, with the most long-lived of 
them over a millennia old. Much of that time is spent 
in hibernation, usually in a cave or underground lair.
Dragons come in a staggering diversity of colors, 
suggesting several different types. But dragons are 
all one kind. Their color is a mere environmental 
adaptation to camouflage them from their enemies 
and prey. Within a year of migrating to a new 
environment, a dragon grows new scales under 
its old ones, which then flake off. During this 
transformation, it’s not uncommon to hear reports of 
a dragon of one color with large patches of another 
color showing through. The adaptation is not only 
scale-deep, as dragons may grow or lose webbed claws, 
horns, gills, and more. Swapping one breath weapon 
for another is yet another adaptation.
Each dragon is an individual, evincing a wide array 
of disposition and personality among dragonkind. 
Some are craven and crafty while others are gregarious 
and sociable. Those who live near people and are so 
inclined learn to change shape to move freely among 
cities, villages, and tribes.
Variant Trait: Change Shape
An ancient or adult dragon that lives near settlements or 
other sizeable groups of people adds the following trait to its 
stat block:
Change Shape. The dragon magically polymorphs into a 
person that has a challenge score no higher than its own, or 
back into its true form. It reverts to its true form if it dies. Any 
equipment it is wearing or carrying is absorbed or borne by the 
new form (the dragon’s choice).
In a new form, the dragon retains its health pool, Health Dice, 
ability to articulate, proficiencies, Legendary Resistance, lair 
actions, and Intelligence, Wisdom, and Presence, as well as this 
action. Its statistics and capabilities are otherwise replaced by 
those of the new form, except any step features or legendary 
actions of that form.
D
Dragonborn:
The dragonborn were breathed into life by Ulruth 
and Ayraed at the same time as the kobolds and 
dragons in a time when they weren’t enemies bound to 
destroy each other. The dragonborn and kobolds were 
originally created to aid the dragons in their grand 
plans for the world, and for a time the dragonborn 
followed that path, dedicating their lives to the whims 
and goals of their dragon overlords.
However, as time went on it was clear that the 
dragons’ goals and whims were petty things or 
completely disregarded their lives. The different 
dragonborn clans banded together, and either through 
words or blood, left the service of the dragons to live 
life as they saw fit. When they left the dragons, they 
also turned their backs on the gods that created them 
to be subjugated and left them in the clutches of such 
petty and uncaring beings.
The People
Dragonborns look like the humanoid form of their 
previous masters. They are covered in scales of a 
variety of colors. Most of them don’t have tails, but 
some do. They have talons on their hands and feet.
Clan before everything else. That is the core tenet of 
being a dragonborn. In all their dealings, dragonborns 
remember that their deeds reflect on all those that 
share their clan names. The greatest affront is to do 
something that shames their clan. 
The majority of dragonborns spend their lives inside 
dragonborn havens where their customs are the norm. 
The dragonborn who live outside are often diplomats, 
adventurers, or exiles. Those who make a life outside 
oftentimes still believe in the ways of their people and 
follow all of the customs, even if they aren’t around 
others of their kind. The exception to that are exiles, 
and that depends on why they were exiled.

their freedom. They left the cities where so much pain 
and cruelty occurred, starting new ones both on the 
surface and underground. Some did stay in the city 
and continued to worship the goddess, never knowing 
anything else and not wanting anything else.
The People
Drow typically have white or silver hair and darkened 
skin ranging from dark purple to obsidian black. Their 
eyes are red, gray, violet, or yellow. 
Those who abandoned their goddess scattered 
throughout the land, creating or joining new 
communities. There was some initial hostility, 
especially from communities that had been directly 
impacted by the drow’s previous behavior. But in time, 
that eased. 
The drow who live in mixed-ancestry communities 
either try to keep to themselves or be pillars of the 
community. They’ve abandoned all the cultural 
practices they once had and adopted the ones of their 
new community.
The drow who created new communities kept a lot 
of their cultural practices to still feel some connection 
to their roots but modified them to reflect their 
progress. Those who live in secluded areas are self-
sustained and try to stay out of sight of other groups 
of people. The ones that surfaced near others opened 
up trade, sending ambassadors and trying to be a part 
of the community at large.

Dwarves:
Created from the stone of the earth by Thorfet, the 
Great Creator, and Azzirra the AllMother, dwarves 
have always been attuned with the earth, being able 
to easily and deftly find and manipulate all of its 
treasures.
The People
Dwarves are among the shortest of all the peoples, 
individuals standing between four and five feet tall. 
They come in every range of skin tones from the palest 
of whites to the darkest of browns. They typically have 
very kinky hair in shades of reds, browns, and blacks.

Eagles:
An eagle is a sizable and powerful bird of prey. 
Their long, broad wings contribute to their swift 
aerial speeds, and their large, hooked beaks easily 
tear into prey. Eagles are known for their incredibly 
keen eyesight. They can be found in many different 
habitats, from dense woodlands to populated lakes to 
mountainous regions.
A giant eagle is a noble creature that understands 
speech. A mated pair of giant eagles typically has up 
to four eggs or young in their nest. Aside from their 
size and greater intelligence, giant eagles display 
habits similar to their smaller counterparts—though 
they hunt far larger creatures and nest at far higher 
altitudes.

Elementals:
The fundamental, primordial elements that make 
up existence are air, earth, fire, and water. There 
are planes of existence that embody only one 
each, but also areas throughout the planes that 
resonate specifically with one of them. In these 
areas, elementals can form. These spirits are each 
manifestations of the primeval element that spawned 
them, living extensions of those forces that embody 
the element’s traits.
They interact with their environment and other 
creatures in accordance to those traits. For example, 
fire elementals can blaze with destruction or provide 
life-giving warmth, while water elementals can as 
easily drown travelers as they can rejuvenate and carry 
them to safety. Earth elementals cause landslides 
and provide shelter to wandering creatures, and air 
elementals create thundering squalls and slow the 
descent of plummeting people. While they carry 
within them the potential of primordial devastation, 
elementals also bear the nurturing aspects of their 
incarnate element.
A trained spellcaster can call upon the service of an 
elemental. Oftentimes, this practice is used to assist 
in combat or with another task befitting the specific 
elemental summoned—such as a fire elemental 
providing heat for a furnace or an earth elemental 
clearing a cave-in. Some spellcasters forcibly bind an 
elemental’s assistance, while others have found ways to 
entreat the spirits for aid without compulsion.

Elves:
Elves were created by the great elven pantheon 
to bring beauty, knowledge and protection to the 
world. The high elves were tasked with creating and 
discovering knowledge while the wood elves were 
tasked with protecting the forest.
The People
Elves have unearthly grace and features. Despite 
resembling humans in a lot of ways, from skin tone to 
hair and eye variation, their unnatural beauty makes 
them appear beyond human.
High elven society focused on beauty and 
knowledge, specifically arcane knowledge. Many 
high elves can cast at least one spell from a young 
age. Older high elves often learn how to create 
a masterwork piece of art that, once made, they 
carry with them the rest of their days. Once those 
milestones are passed, the elf in question decides the 
best way to spend their long life—creating works of 
beauty or furthering their arcane prowess.
A wood elf’s life is a constant test in the wild. A test 
of their foraging skills, of their hunting skills, of their 
fighting skills. They often are perfectly attuned to the 
forest and able to draw upon the inherent magic of the 
land to aid them. While they are wary of outsiders, 
they are seldom hostile unless given a reason to be.

Frogs:
Frogs are short-bodied, tailless amphibians with long 
tongues and skin whose coloration can range between 
muted to vivid hues. They have a wide range of 
habitats, from tropical to arctic regions, and typically 
dwell near water, in trees, or underground. As 
carnivores, frogs feed on insects. They are able to leap 
significant distances. Giant frogs occur in areas with a 
high exposure to magic and, if threatened, engage in 
combat, unlike their smaller relatives. If its prey or an 
opponent is small enough, a giant frog doesn’t hesitate 
to swallow it whole.
Toads are a subspecies of frogs known for their dry, 
leathery skin covered in bumps, shorter legs, and a 
preference toward less aquatic habitats. Giant toads 
fight similarly to giant frogs, but are overall more 
dangerous because of their greater durability and 
poisonous bite.

Fungi:
Fungi are found throughout the Material Planes 
and grow by feasting on dead matter, ideally in dark 
and moist conditions. However, when fungi grow 
in regions awash with heavy magic or from feeding 
on deceased magical creatures, they can develop 
sentience and cultivate new and unusual properties. 
These magical mushrooms are often indistinguishable 
from their nonmagical counterparts until aggravated. 
Two of these fungi are known as shriekers—named 
for the unbearable sound they emit in the presence 
of creatures or light—and violet fungus—who have 
limited mobility and can rot the flesh of creatures 
they touch.

Genies:
Genies are mature primordial spirits that were once 
mere elementals. After centuries of unique experiences 
with other creatures, an elemental can manifest a 
more physical form and greater intelligence. These 
powerful elemental spirits—now genies—roam 
beyond the boundaries of the realms that bore them 
to collect greater and wider things. While some genies 
eventually tire of roaming and return to a primordial 
realm to make their permanent residence, others never 
settle and instead partake of the hospitality of the 
world for as long as they can.
Ancient sorcerers long tried to bind genies to 
their service, and some have never forgotten that 
transgression. Those genies nurse a contempt of 
mortalkind and either refuse to help people or are 
outright hostile toward them. Genies are capable 
fighters and spellcasters in their own right, and fight 
with guile and creativity. When a genie dies, it returns 
to the elemental energy that spawned it, leaving 
nothing but its material possessions as its spirit rejoins 
the elemental force.
Djinn
Djinn are genies manifested from air elementals. They 
are swift creatures, with lightning-fast movements and 
the power of storms at their command. As collectors, 
djinn roam the world searching for unique, priceless 
treasures—keeping their favorites and trading others. 
Their homes are typically found at the heights of the 
world, in permanently stormy regions, or atop the 
very clouds. Djinn put their collections on display 
and earnestly show them off and detail their history to 
interested parties. A person seeking a boon or one of 
a djinni’s treasures should bring something one-of-a-
kind as a gift of courtesy or to trade.

Ghouls:
Ghouls are ferocious undead created when the soul 
of an unintelligent beast is bound to the corpse of a 
mortal person by means of necromantic magic. Near-
feral creatures that lurk the boundaries of graveyards 
and battlefields, ghouls readily feast upon corpses and 
make new meals out of unsuspecting victims that draw 
too close to their feeding grounds. They fight with 
teeth and claws—the latter of which are infected and 
seizes creatures afflicted by them.
If a monster’s soul is used in the process to create 
a ghoul, the corpse instead rises as a ghast. More 
powerful than a ghoul, a ghast is surrounded by 
a sickening aura and exerts influence over ghouls, 
creating packs. A pack of ghouls are deadly scavengers, 
and the presence of a ghast makes them far less 
susceptible to divine rebuke.

Giants:
The statuesque giants are a timeworn people whose 
civilizations once sprawled across the Material Planes 
and beyond. Vast calamities and sweeping wars 
shaped the realms and brought the giants down from 
the height of their empire. In their wake, they left 
numerous monolithic cities and fortresses as little 
more than abandoned ruins, rich with history to be 
discovered by today’s civilizations.
Yet the giants persist in the remote regions of 
the world. A people united in soul but divided by 
bloodlines; each giant’s lineage has an affinity to 
a force of nature—from the fury of storms to the 
arctic cold to the rolling hills themselves. While they 
were once a people of disparate nations, the giants 
came together to ensure their ways and traditions 
survived. Their communities vary between reclusivity 
for preservation, animosity toward smaller folk for 
supplanting the giants, and earnestness to welcome 
and share their culture with other people. Other 
giants have taken to the world to search the ruins of 
their ancestors and uncover anything they can use or 
preserve.
Cloud Giant
From their affinity with the stormless sky, cloud 
giants are blessed with innate magic through their 
bloodline. Drawing upon that magic, they can fly 
with ease, summon rolling fogs, transform their own 
bodies into mists, and even influence the weather. 
While cloud giants are well-known for their peaceable 
temperament, their patience isn’t without limits. Even 
clear skies can portent an overcast day.

Gnomes:
Gnomes believe they share an origin with dwarves, 
having emerged from the earth. However, their origins 
diverge slightly as gnomes specifically believe their 
ancestors were birthed from the gems the earth held. 
None are quite sure how true this is and even their 
current gods aren’t aware, as they were once mortal 
and elevated by the faith of their people.
The People
Much like dwarves, gnomes are among the shortest of 
all peoples. They’ve got plumb faces and prominent 
noses. Their skin tones typically range from tan to 
dark brown, their eyes are on the lighter side, and 
their hair is shockingly vibrant.
Much like the dwarves, gnomes are known for 
their great craftsmanship, specifically in regards to 
clockwork mechanism and constructs. Unlike the 
dwarves, they don’t create things to venerate a god, 
but simply to appease their own curious nature and 
one-up their friends.
Due to their competitive drive, large creation 
celebrations are held quarterly throughout the year 
with the winner being crowned the Monarch of 
Creation. The monarch is treated with the deference 
due to royalty until a new one is crowned. However, 
unless qualified to rule, their opinion on government 
matters is politely ignored.

Goats are hoofed mammals recognizable for their 
horns. They are one of the first domesticated animals 
for the resources they can provide—labor, milk, meat,

goats. Their herbivorous diet includes varied plantlife. 
Domestic goats are found throughout the Material 
Planes, but wild goats are typically found at high 
elevations. Their horns are useful weapons, and the 
subspecies of giant goats use them to dangerous effect, 
especially when charging a perceived threat.
