Goblinoids:
Bugbears, goblins and hobgoblins were created to be 
mighty warriors, generals, and spies for Krolzenor 
the Red General. Krolzenor wanted dominion over 
all the gods and peoples. A great war was fought and 
Krolzenor was defeated, in part by his own creation 
who didn’t want to die just so he could rule. Millennia 
passed and now the bugbears, goblins, and hobgoblins 
live their lives as they see fit.
The People
Bugbears resemble hairy, muscular, and overgrown 
goblins, often standing well over six feet tall. Their 
nose and claws resemble those of bears, but the claws 
aren’t sharp enough to be used as weapons.
They are solitary creatures. You’re unlikely to see 
bugbears in large groups unless they’ve been employed 
by others to work together. At most, they travel in 
groups of three, and when that happens, it’s often two 
parents and their child. Left to their own devices, they 
wander from place to place taking in the scenery and 
culture. 
Goblins are short, round-faced people with green 
skin. They have coarse, often short hair and their eyes 
are typically dark brown, nearly black.
They surround themselves with other goblins. 
A family often consists of grandparents, parents, 
siblings, and any children. While the majority of the 
families are goblins, it isn’t unusual to see adopted 
hobgoblins and bugbears among them. When living in 
a neighborhood made up primarily of goblins, it feels 
like one large extended family. 
Hobgoblins are large and muscled with fur-covered 
bodies. Their fur is often reddish-brown, gray, or 
orange. They’re, on average, around six and a half 
feet tall. 
They value order and a strict hierarchy. Their 
communities are structured as such and the day-to-
day lives are very orderly. Each hour some type of 
signal, usually a bell or drums, is heard throughout the 
community in order to keep them on schedule. They 
do have unstructured hours, typically after the work 
day. Hobgoblins who were raised in communities but 
move to mixed-ancestry communities take a while to 
acclimate to the change.

Grimlock:
The ancestors of grimlocks were humans who made 
caves and tunnels their home. Like most creatures who 
live underground in the total dark for generations, the 
grimlock became pale and lost their sight. Grimlock 
are born without eyes and adapted to rely on their 
other senses to navigate their subterranean territory. 
They are mostly hairless as well.
The People
People sometimes tell scary stories of grimlocks, but 
grimlocks are no more deadly than their surface-
dwelling counterparts. They have the same mix of 
benevolence and malice as humans do. Grimlocks 
cultivate vast lichen and mushroom farms, fish in 
underground lakes and streams, and hunt beasts 
and monsters who live in the dark. Close quarters 
underground has made grimlocks more patient and 
familiar with each other than members of most other 
peoples. They tend to sit down and resolve their 
differences rather than let them boil over, since leaving 
the group to strike out on one’s own is usually fatal.

in Perception.

Hags:
Whispered of as crones and witches, hags are said 
to be evil incarnate. Lurking in their dark lairs, they 
devour children, corrupt wayward women, and 
deceive and destroy anyone else. Daughters are warned 
to act properly and littles one to behave, lest they be 
snatched up by the hags of dark stories and cautionary 
tales. After all, no one wants to be as hideous as a hag, 
nor devoured in the woods. But these stories told of 
hags do not reveal the whole truth. 
People are frightened of hags—but not about what 
they claim. The truth is that hags are women who 
refuse to be complicit and quiet. They choose bargains 
with the fey and other powers, trading their “prized” 
beauty for strength, over being prey to the whims 
and desires of unjust and corrupt systems. Hags are 
apostates and rebels who undermine evil that goes 
unseen.
A hag shelters women abandoned and disgraced 
for wanting their own path, rescues children from 
uncaring households, and torments those who would 
make others suffer through their own deception. It 
cannot be said that some hags do not live up to their 
reputation, but the vast majority seek to right the 
injustices they first ran from, no matter the cost. 
Green Hag
Green hags make their homes in twilit woods and 
gloomy swamps near the towns and cities they seek to 
subvert. Their uncanny ability to mimic the sounds 
of animals and people allow them to disrupt hunters 
and heroes searching for them or the children under 
their protection. Green hags can make themselves 
invisible and almost untrackable, further confounding 
those who hunt them. While their illusory magic does 
not hold up to inspection, green hags can disguise 
themselves enough to buy supplies from towns or keep 
an ear to the plights of those they would seek to aid.

Half-Dragon:
Half-dragons do not share the divine origins that 
the other draconic lineages do. They’re created from 
dalliances between polymorphed dragons and other 
creatures. Their worship of Ayraed and Ulruth vary 
widely depending on where they grew up, which 
parent they grew up with, and their dragon parent’s 
own attitude towards the draconic gods.
The People
Half-dragons resemble their non-dragon parent but 
have the scales of their dragon parent on various parts 
of their body. They can be clearly visible, covering 
more than half of their body, or barely visible, only 
appearing in discrete places. They can have sharpened 
teeth and claws, or even wings.
Half-dragons belong to two worlds. Some half-
dragons hide their heritage and try to blend in with 
their non-draconic heritage. Others embrace their 
draconic heritage and the ego that comes with it, 
thriving to become someone whose name strikes awe, 
fear, and respect.
Dragonborn. Those who know the history of 
the dragons and dragonborn would think there was 
animosity between the half-dragons and dragonborn, 
but most dragonborn hail them as cousins, and some 
half-dragons have found themselves welcomed into 
dragonborn clans.
Kobolds. Half-dragons are treated like royalty, 
especially if they are the child of the dragon the 
kobolds serve. They can live among the community 
and feel right at home, even if they are the tallest 
member there.

Living Constructs:
A living construct is a vessel, constructed in the shape 
of a person, to house a spark of life imbued by magic. 
Living constructs are not sentient, being created by 
spellcasters in order to carry out timeless duties, such 
as protecting a sacred place or town of innocents, 
on behalf of their creator. They differ from animated 
objects in that they are not merely enchanted to act 
and are not rendered inert by fields of antimagic. 
The strength of a living construct depends on the 
quality of material that goes into it, the proficiency of 
the artisan that crafts the vessel, and the skill of the 
spellcaster that imbues it with life. 
Clay and flesh are particularly fickle substances. A 
homunculus made of flesh is not only horrifying to 
behold, but also extremely vulnerable to fire. Both a 
homunculus of flesh and golem made of clay have a 
chance to go berserk if their vessel is damaged enough, 
as it puts the living construct’s magical spark in 
jeopardy. Though harder to procure and shape, both 
stone and iron are much more protective materials 
and make for sturdier constructs. All living constructs, 
due to the process used in their creation, are heavily 
resistant to magic and cannot have their forms altered 
by it. 
The magic that goes into creating a living construct 
also imbues it with magical strength and other 
abilities—such as surprising attacking speed in a 
golem or poisonous gas in an iron construct. While 
living constructs are imbued with the ability to follow 
instructions and carry out tasks, they are not intended 
to be individuals with consciousness. Some archmages 
have striven to change this, attempting to create living 
constructs with sentience, but such experiments are 
controversial.
Lizards:
Lizards are widespread reptiles and can be found in 
every habitat throughout the Material Planes. They 
range in size from the span of a halfling’s finger to the 
length of a troll, not counting the giant subspecies 
typically found in magical jungles and in subterranean 
habitats. Lizards are generally carnivores, though 
some species are known to be omnivores or even 
herbivores. They have countless deterrents against 
predators—from venom to camouflage to sacrificing 
and regrowing their own tails. A giant lizard can be 
ridden or used as a draft animal. Subterranean giant 
lizards are used as mounts and pack animals by many 
people.

have taken. As such, they make natural guides, scouts, 
and explorers.
On the Material Planes, minotaurs often live 
in remote places, building small communities of 
minotaurs and those friendly to them. Their ability 
to find their way back home allows them to live 
in the most trackless places. Most who enjoy the 
hospitality of minotaurs never find their way back for 
a return visit.
Minotaurs’ stature makes them formidable 
opponents, and those who choose the soldier, warrior, 
or mercenary life are usually successful. Just as many 
minotaurs have a gentle disposition, content to 
ruminate about the multiverse and its many wonders.

Mummy:
Under the right conditions—whether due to magic, 
the right environment, or the ancient embalming 
arts—the corpse of a person or beast can be preserved 
as a mummy. The process of mummification can be 
incidental or a deliberate cultural act performed after 
a creature’s death. When a mummy is intentionally 
made, the organs are removed and the body is 
carefully embalmed, wrapped, and sealed away.
Due to their unique preservation, mummies are 
especially resistant to being raised by necromancy. 
As such, spellcasters invested in the necromantic arts 
have devised a ritual specifically to raise mummified 
corpses. While magic animates the bodies—whose 
knowledge, skills, and magic they knew in life are 
also preserved—it has the unintentional side effect of 
cursing the undead creatures with a debilitating gaze 
and a malignant curse, one they could pass to others 
and would turn its victims to dust if not removed. 
Given the extensive rituals needed to raise one, 
mummies are rare. Their potent abilities and 
intelligence make them advantageous guardians, or 
even consultants, for the spellcasters who are able 
to create them, though few mummies relish their 
undead fate.
Mummy Template
This template can be applied to any beast or person 
stat block. The creature keeps all its statistics, except as 
noted below.
Type. The mummy’s type is undead.
Armor Scraps. The mummy’s defense score is 12 + 
its Agility.
Speed. The mummy loses any flying or swimming 
speed, and its speed is 20 feet.
Abilities. The mummy’s Strength increases by 3, 
and its Agility decreases by 1.
Saving Checks. The mummy gains proficiency in 
Wisdom saving checks.
Vulnerabilities, Resistances, and Immunities. 
The mummy gains vulnerability to fire damage; 
resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing 
from nonmagical attacks; and immunity to necrotic 
and poison damage and the enraptured, exhaustion, 
frightened, inert, and sickened conditions.
Senses. The mummy’s primary sense is sight, and it 
gains darkvision out to a range of 60 feet.
New Action: Rotting Fist. The mummy can attack 
with its fist, inflicting bludgeoning damage equal to 
2d6 + their Strength plus 3d6 necrotic damage on a 
hit. If the target is a creature, it must succeed on a 
Health saving check (DS = 8 + the mummy's Health 
+ their proficiency bonus) or be cursed with mummy
rot. The cursed target can’t replenish any health drops,
and its health pool depth decreases by 10 (3d6) for
every 24 hours that elapse. If the curse destroys the
target’s health pool, the target dies, and its body turns
to dust. The curse lasts until removed by the remove
curse spell or other magic.
New Action: Dreadful Glare. The mummy targets 
one creature it can see within 60 feet of it. If the target 
can see the mummy, it must succeed on a Wisdom 
saving check (DS = 8 + the mummy's Presence + 
their proficiency bonus) against this magic or become 
frightened until the end of the mummy’s next turn. If 
the target fails the saving check by 5 or more, it is also 
inert for the same duration. A target that succeeds on 
the saving check is immune to the Dreadful Glare of 
all mummies for the next 24 hours.

Nagas:
Many believe the naga came from the sea—legends say 
that the long-living creatures were the first to come 
from its waters, exploring the unmapped lands of the 
early worlds and seeking to understand the magic 
inherent in them. Much of that history has been 
lost to time; nowadays, what is known of the naga is 
that they are deeply magical. These ancient creatures, 
which bear people’s heads atop their long, serpentine 
form, are found in the deepest parts of ruins and 
wildernesses, where they guard, seek, or manipulate 
arcane secrets.
The nagas’ ability to return to life after they are 
slain is what makes them keepers of some of the most 
ancient of secrets. They are cunning spellcasters whose 
venomous bite is a last resort to protect themselves. 
Immensely solitary and secretive creatures, it is rare 
to find one, let alone a group. Many people who 
encounter a naga, however, come back knowing a 
once-buried occult secret—whether for good or for 
gravely ill.

body and eight tentacles. They make their habitats 
throughout the ocean, from the abyssal depths,

of their skin to blend in with their surroundings.

magic and can be mistaken for krakens by especially 
nervous and jittery sailors.

Oozes:
A veteran adventurer’s first advice to a junior can be 
many things, among them “beware of any ancient 
place with spotless floors and walls—for an ooze surely 
lurks nearby.” Amorphous, viscous creatures, oozes 
are unintelligent predators that consume any and all 
organic material they can find, and are often found in 
ruins and dungeons where scavenging creatures and 
plantlife thrive…and unwitting adventurers frequently 
stumble into.
Oozes are said to have originated from an 
alchemical experiment gone awry—though others 
claim they are the demonic discharge of greater abyssal 
monsters that wield slime and acid against their foes. 
Whatever their true beginnings, it is certainly possible 
that with enough latent magic and planar energy 
seeping into unnatural muck that oozes gained life 
and, more than that, an insatiable hunger.

Rats:
The scurrying of rodents is a common sound wherever 
people gather. Rats are small mammals found 
throughout the Material Planes, but especially in 
the bustling hearts of civilization. As opportunistic 
scavengers, rats find it beneficial to be where people 
are, plucking their meals from the waste left behind 
by their larger neighbors. Rats make their homes in 
sewers, abandoned buildings, and other dark, remote 
areas. They are nocturnal, and use the cover of night 
to remain out of sight while finding food.
A rat’s teeth are strong enough to chew through 
wood and metal, with the infamous and vexing giant 
rats able to chew through even thicker materials. Rats 
are prone to carrying and passing on virulent diseases, 
and they often gather in swarms—which allow them 
to overwhelm enemies when they are antagonized. 
Plenty of fledgling adventurers are tasked with ridding 
local establishments of the nuisance of these oversized 
or congregating pests.

Sahuagin:
Like merfolk, sahuagin are also a people of the sea, but 
their origins are tied to the merfolk’s need to protect 
others at all cost. After a particularly dangerous war 
with an aboleth and their minions that decimated 
a number of merfolk towns and cities, a group of 
wizards concocted a spell that would transform 
willing merfolk into stronger versions of themselves. 
Hundreds volunteered and the first sahuagin 
were born.
Initially they did their duty well, giving their 
lives to protect their fellow merfolk, but eventually 
many sahuagin grew unhappy with how their lives 
were treated as expendable compared to the merfolk 
warriors who hadn’t undergone the change. The 
sahuagin rebelled, killing the wizards who knew the 
spell to create more sahuagin and striking out on 
their own.
The People
Sahuagin are very muscular. They’ve got horns and a 
membrane all over their body, with spikes protruding 
from them. They’ve also got powerful spiked tails and 
dark black eyes.
Due to the way the merfolk treated them, they’ve 
viewed them as their most hated enemies. After the 
rebellion, there was a time when they would raid 
merfolk cities and towns for supplies and revenge. 
Because of these actions, the merfolk in turn saw them 
as hated enemies.
The sahuagin live a nomadic life, not by choice, 
but out of necessity. Despite the fact that they bear 
many children, sahuagin are outnumbered by merfolk 
almost ten to one, and whenever one group comes 
across the other, fighting ensues with devastating 
losses on both sides, but more so for the sahuagin.
Due to this bitter rivalry, it's common to find 
sahuagin communities on the coast or traveling among 
sailing ships.

Scorpions:
Scorpions are carnivorous arachnids, recognizable 
for their grasping pincers and forward curving tail 
with a stinger on the end. They are found in many 
different habitats, but primarily in deserts and other 
harsh environments and climates. In order to hunt 
their typical prey—insects and small mammals and 
reptiles—scorpions entrap them in their claws, then 
finish them off by injecting venom through their 
stingers. Giant scorpions are much deadlier and more 
dangerous than typical scorpions, with venom that can 
easily kill the average person. They are generally found 
in subterranean or desert caverns during the day, then 
stalk their chosen habitats during the night to hunt 
for any meaty creatures.

Sharks:

the waters for telltale fins, sharks are aquatic apex 
predators that inhabit the seas. Their carnivorous 
diets typically include fish, crustaceans, and marine 
mammals, but can extend to people. While usually

sharks. Keen and swift hunters, most sharks are 
solitary beasts, but certain types—such as the small 
reef shark, which inhabits shallower waters and coral

are found in deep oceans. Utterly fearless, they prey 
on anything that crosses their path, including whales 
and seafaring people. Some aquatic peoples, such as 
merrows, train sharks as companions.

Skeleton:
The telltale clattering of bones strikes fear into the 
hearts of adventurers, usually serving as a warning 
for whatever danger lurks ahead. Those bones might 
be moving of their own accord, rattling in malicious 
pursuit. Skeletons are the byproduct of necromantic 
magics raising corpses that are so old as to be reduced 
to mere bones. 
While skeletons can be raised intentionally, they are 
often the byproduct of dark magics gradually building 
up in an area of great death and tragedy, such as an 
ancient battlefield or a castle abandoned because of 
plague. The average skeleton retains only a vestigial 
sense of self, enough to recall weapon skills and innate 
magic but little else. Skeletons are faster than zombies 
due to being unburdened by injured flesh and muscle, 
but their exposed bones are brittle and vulnerable to 
well-placed brute force.

knowledge of its former life. It loses any spellcasting 
ability the base creature might have had, but it retains 
its Innate Spellcasting, if any.

it knew in life but can’t speak.

Snakes:
The snake is a carnivorous reptile with a long, 
sinuous body lacking limbs. They are found in diverse 
habitats, ranging from forests and jungles to prairies 
and deserts, with some species even dwelling in and 
around water. While their exact diet is dependent on 
species, snakes are known to eat mammals, insects, 
amphibians, fish, and other reptiles. Giant snakes eat 
prey more appropriate to their size, including people. 
Snakes swallow their prey whole, even if it is much 
larger than they are, and different kinds of snakes 
subdue their meals differently.
Constrictor snakes coil their body around prey and 
suffocate them; they often grow to massive sizes even 
outside of magical regions. Venomous snakes use 
their fangs to inject venom, which grows more potent 
the bigger they are. It is not unheard of for swarms 
of venomous snakes to be used in traps or defenses. 
A flying snake is a brightly colored, winged serpent 
found in jungles. People sometimes domesticate 
flying snakes to serve as messengers that deliver scrolls 
wrapped in their coils.

Sphinxes:
Enigmatic creatures with the body of a lion, the wings 
of an eagle, and the face of a person, sphinxes are 
thought to be the creations of gods of knowledge or 
magic. They are notably inscrutable, with minds that 
are labyrinthine and unknowable to mortals—even 
through use of magic—and are capable of sensing and 
misdirecting divination. 
Ferociously strong and keenly intelligent, sphinxes 
are divided into the smaller gnosisphinxes and 
the larger, and more powerful, sophisphinxes. A 
sophisphinx’s thrice-bellowed roar can plant terror and 
torpor in the strongest-willed creatures, even while 
rupturing eardrums. All sphinxes are known for their 
extensive knowledge of useful and restorative spells. 
It is rumored in old tales that one suffering from an 
affliction or curse can trade valuable knowledge to a 
sphinx in exchange for a cure.
Sphinxes are often charged with guarding 
repositories of ancient knowledge or powerful magical 
artifacts—either by the gods that created them 
or spellcasters they have made deals with. Often 
these charges are meant to protect the unworthy or 
foolish from gaining access, rather than keeping all 
individuals at bay. As such, sphinxes prefer to judge 
the worth of would-be heroes through tests of wit, 
knowledge, and wisdom over tests of combat.

Spiders:
A spider is a predatory arachnid that uses a sticky 
substance to weave webs to entrap their prey. Normal-
sized spiders typically prey upon insects, fellow 
spiders, or sometimes larger beasts, such as small birds 
and lizards. Some spiders are slightly venomous, but 
giant spiders have a venom that is deadlier to people. 
Much how their smaller kin snare their prey, a giant 
spider spins elaborate webs or shoots sticky strands 
of webbing from their abdomen. Giant spiders are 
most commonly found underground, making their 
lairs on ceilings or in dark, web-filled crevices. Such 
lairs are often festooned with web cocoons holding 
past victims. Smaller than a giant spider, a giant wolf 
spider hunts across open ground or hides in a burrow, 
crevice, or hidden cavity beneath debris.
While specific conditions or magic can influence 
the growth of a giant spider, magical influence can 
also imbue spiders with unusual abilities, such as 
those seen in phase spiders. A phase spider possesses 
the magical ability to phase in and out of the Ethereal 
Plane. They seem to appear out of nowhere and 
quickly vanish after attacking. Their movement on the 
Ethereal Plane before coming back to a material plane 
makes them seem to teleport.

Vampires:
There are several accounts of the origins of vampires. 
One is that the curse was inflicted upon decadent 
mortals by judgmental fiends, another is that they 
were first raised by a bloodthirsty death god, and yet 
others claim mortal necromancers created the unholy 
affliction themselves. What is known and true is that 
vampires are undead who retain their intelligence 
and identity, but have an appetite for blood that they 
must sate lest they wither to dust. The fanged bite of a 
vampire allows them to pierce the flesh of victims and 
drain their blood.
The curse of vampirism grants its victims incredible 
strength, as well as innate powers, such as the ability 
to transform into a bat and regenerate from near-
fatal injuries. However, the curse also confers unusual 
weaknesses, like an incredible vulnerability to sunlight 
and running water.
Many vampires prey on victims in the night, then 
hide during the day, stirring up chaos and confusion 
when bodies drained of blood turn up. Others use 
their might to gather power and wealth, lording over 
townsfolk who fear their influence, power, and hunger. 
Yet, not all vampires survive by wickedness. Some 
subsist on the less nourishing blood of animals to 
avoid causing harm and help others rather than reign 
over them. While many good-intentioned vampires 
hide what they are for fear of scorn, others embrace it 
and are embraced in turn.
A vampire’s bite carries the curse of vampirism, 
and a creature that succumbs to it rises as a vampire 
spawn. While driven by the same thirst for blood and 
limited by the same weaknesses as a regular vampire, 
a spawn does not have the same powers. The vampire 
that created the spawn can elevate them to true 
vampirehood, so spawn that seek power and don’t 
despise their state serve their vampire sire or madam 
in hopes of cultivating enough favor to ascend.

Vultures:
Vultures are scavenger birds that are easily recognized 
by their bald heads, which help keep them clean 
while they feast on carrion. They are primarily found 
in deserts, savannas, and grasslands. A vulture’s wide 
wingspan allows them to glide for hours, either while 
seeking food or waiting for a future meal to die. A 
giant vulture has advanced intelligence. Unlike its 
smaller kin, it attacks a wounded creature to hasten 
its end. Giant vultures have been known to pursue a 
thirsty, starving creature for days. Given that vultures 
devour carcasses and often gather in flocks around 
them, vultures are sometimes considered omens 
of death.

Weasels:
The small, sleek weasel is a carnivorous mammal that 
is a far more dangerous predator than it appears. 
Their long body allows weasels to follow prey into 
their burrows. As cunning hunters, they can kill 
prey that is much bigger than them, such as squirrels 
and rabbits. Weasels thrive in fields, woodlands, and 
thickets, as well as near farmlands, where they are 
often considered vermin for their tendency to steal 
chicken and eggs. While typically not aggressive 
toward people, they attack if frightened. Giant weasels 
are uncommon, but they have a far more voracious 
appetite than their smaller kind, and as such, are a 
much greater nuisance to communities with larger 
livestock and other tempting resources.

Wolves:
Wolves are widespread canines and predators. Found 
in habitats—including forests, grasslands, deserts, 
tundras, and mountains—throughout the Material 
Planes, they hunt deer, sheep, and bison, along with 
smaller mammals when large prey is scarce. They 
gather in packs, allowing them to hunt much larger 
animals than they could alone. Known for their loyalty 
and ferocity, it is not uncommon to find wolves as the 
companions of rangers and other adventurers. Dire 
wolves are much larger wolves, hardier and stronger 
than their regular-sized kin. They can survive in much 
harsher environments, and packs of dire wolves prey 
on beasts and monsters like mammoths and chimeras.
The arctic-dwelling winter wolf is as large as a 
dire wolf but has snow-white fur and pale blue eyes. 
Frost giants use these creatures as guards and hunting 
companions, putting the wolves’ deadly breath 
weapon to use against their foes. Winter wolves 
communicate with one another telepathically, but 
they understand Giant well enough to follow simple 
conversations.

Zombie:
On a bloodied battlefield, a fallen combatant lurches 
once more to their feet under the incantations of a 
dark-robed figure—and the zombie lurches forward in 
spite of the gaping wound across its stomach toward 
the necromancer’s nearest foe. Zombies are raised 
by necromantic magics from corpses that have not 
fully skeletonized. While they are some of the easiest 
undead to raise, they are often slower and weaker 
than their living selves due to the bloated and fatally 
wounded state of their bodies.
Moreover, a zombie generally loses all sense of 
its previous identity, including any trained skills or 
spellcasting it once knew. As a result, zombies are 
generally simple-minded and thus easy to outwit, 
though they single-mindedly pursue tasks given to 
them by the necromancer that raised them or another 
powerful force that exerts control over them. Due to 
their relentless nature and uncanny endurance, which 
allows them to sometimes ignore lethal blows, zombies 
are often raised in hordes to overwhelm opponents or 
objectives.
Zombie Template
This template can be applied to any aberration, beast, 
giant, monster, or person stat block. The creature 
keeps its statistics, except as follows.
Type. The zombie’s type is undead.
Defense Score. The zombie’s defense is 10 + its 
Agility. 
Speed. The zombie reduces each of its speeds by 
10 feet.
Abilities. Replace the base creature’s abilities with 
the following: its Agility is −2, its Health increases 
by 1, its Intelligence is −3, its Wisdom is −2, and its 
Presence is −3.
Saving Checks. The zombie gains proficiency in 
Wisdom saving checks.
Immunities. The zombie gains immunity to poison 
damage and the sickened condition.
Senses. The zombie’s primary sense is sight, and it 
gains darkvision out to a range of 60 feet.
Mindless. The zombie loses the memories and 
knowledge of its former life. It loses any spellcasting 
ability the base creature might have had, but it retains 
its Innate Spellcasting, if any.
Undead Fortitude. If damage empties the zombie’s 
health pool, it must make a Health saving check with 
a DS of 5 + the damage suffered, unless the damage is 
radiant or from a critical hit. On a success, the zombie 
retains 1 drop of health instead.
Languages. The zombie understands the languages 
it knew in life but can’t articulate them.
New Action: Slam. A zombie that has limbs and is 
otherwise unarmed can make a slam attack, inflicting 
bludgeoning damage equal to 1d6 + its Strength 
on a hit.

Paired Items:
Items that come in pairs—such as boots, bracers, 
gauntlets, and gloves—impart their benefits only 
if both items of the pair are worn. For example, a 
character wearing a boot of striding and springing on 
one foot and a boot of sylvankind on the other foot 
gains no benefit from either.

Activating an Item:
Activating some magic items requires a user to do 
something special, such as holding the item and 
uttering or signing a command word. The description 
of each item category or individual item details how 
an item is activated. Certain items use the following 
rules for their activation.
If an item requires an action to activate, that action 
isn’t a function of the Use an Item action.
Command Word:
A command word is a word or phrase that must be 
spoken or signed for an item to work. A magic item 
that requires a command word can’t be activated 
vocally in an area where sound is prevented, as in 
the area of the silence spell. Naturally, signing the 
command word still works.
Consumables:
Some items are used up when they are activated. 
A potion or an elixir must be swallowed, or an oil 
applied to the body. The writing vanishes from a scroll 
when it is read. Once used, a consumable item loses 
its magic.

anything contained within it is transported to a

Bag of Holding:
Wondrous item, uncommon
This bag has an interior space considerably larger than 
its outside dimensions, roughly 2 feet in diameter 
at the mouth and 4 feet deep. The bag can hold the 
equivalent of up to 32 item slots. The bag takes up 1 
item slot, regardless of its contents. Retrieving an item

If the bag is overloaded, pierced, or torn, it ruptures

contents spill forth, unharmed, but the bag must

creatures (minimum 1 minute), after which time they 
begin to suffocate.
Placing a bag of holding inside an extradimensional 
space created by a handy haversack, portable hole, or 
similar item instantly destroys both items and opens 
a gate to the Astral Plane. The gate originates where 
the one item was placed inside the other. Any creature 
within 10 feet of the gate is sucked through it to a 
random location on the Astral Plane. The gate then 
closes. The gate is one-way only and can’t be reopened.

sphere until they are no longer inside it. Only 
breathable air can pass through the sphere’s wall. No

An enclosed creature can use its action to push

Appendix A: Spell Lists
These optional spell lists are for spellcasters who want to apply a particular theme to their spellcasting.
Blight Spells
Choose spells from this list 
if you want to meddle in rot, 
decay, putrefaction, and other 
manifestations of entropy.
Cantrips (0 Level)
Curse System:
Strange and powerful curses are abundant in Those 
Who Wander. From the bites of vampires and werefolk 
to the powerful words of hags, there are many ways to 
find yourself cursed with some type of affliction. 
This section aims to provide a robust system for 
players wanting to become a vampire or werefolk, 
along with storyteller rules on how to have hags curse 
people.
Enhancements and
Detriments:
Here are all of the detriments you can apply 
to yourself in order to gain more points to buy 
enhancements.
Aconite Poisoning (Payment Varies). If you ingest 
aconite, a poisonous plant with hooded pink or purple 
flowers, or inhale its fragrance, you suffer the sickened 
condition until you are cured or 5 days have passed. 
While sickened in this way, you suffer 1 level of 
exhaustion that can only be removed after 5 days’ time 
or by magic.
Fire Vulnerability (Payment Varies). You are 
vulnerable to fire damage.
Greater Aconite Poisoning (Requirements: 
Aconite Poisoning; Payment Varies). If you ingest 
aconite or inhale its fragrance, you suffer the sickened 
condition until you are cured or 5 days have passed. 
While sickened in this way, you suffer 2 levels of 
exhaustion that can only be removed after 5 days’ time 
or by magic.
Greater Bloodlust. (Pays 3 Points). The first time 
piercing or slashing damage is inflicted on a living 
creature in combat, you must succeed on a DS 16 
Wisdom saving check or go wild on your next two 
turns, attacking a random living creature within range 
of your overland speed.
Greater Lunar Eclipse. (Payment Varies). You are 
physically weakened by lunar eclipses. You spill half 
your remaining health pool and suffer one level of 
exhaustion that cannot be removed until the full lunar 
eclipse is gone.
Superior Aconite Poisoning (Requirements: 
Greater Aconite Poisoning; Payment Varies). If you 
ingest aconite or inhale its fragrance, you suffer the 
sickened condition until you are cured or 5 days have 
passed. While sickened in this way, you suffer 3 levels 
of exhaustion that can only be removed after 5 days’ 
time or by magic.
Superior Bloodlust (Requirements: Greater 
Bloodlust; Pays 5 Points). The first time piercing 
or slashing damage is inflicted on a living creature 
in combat, you must succeed on a DS 18 Wisdom 
saving check or go wild on your next three turns, 
attacking a random living creature within range of 
your overland speed.
Hag Curses:
This system is completely storyteller-facing. It gives 
you a number of curse examples you can place on 
characters and other nonplayer creatures, ingredients 
with which to create them, and how to cure them. The 
remove curse spell can be used to remove any of these 
curses.
Animal’s Animosity:
Beasts can perceive the target within 30 feet and 
attack them if able.
Ingredients. Fur and the heart for each kind of 
beast the hag wants to attack the cursed. Up to five 
species. 
Cure. You must channel the essence of a nature 
spirit.
Bloodlust:
During combat the target cannot stop fighting until 
every foe is dead. The target even feels compelled to 
kill those that have surrendered or may be useful in 
the future.
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. Blood of a therianthrope or vampire.
Cure. Water from a pool that a unicorn has 
bathed in.
Optional Rule: Remove Curse Ritual
When attempting to remove a curse from an item or individual, 
specific ingredients must be gathered and used while casting 
the spell. You might also need to travel to a specific location, 
depending on the curse. 
When the character is ready to start the ritual, a test of wills 
begins. The character casting remove curse and the hag roll dice. 
The player rolls 1d20 + their spell attack bonus while the hag 
rolls 1d20 + Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma (hag’s choice). 
The creature that wins the most rolls out of 3 wins the contest. A 
hag has advantage if they’re a member of a coven. 
Storytellers can change the number of rolls to suit their needs. 
You can go as low as 1 roll and as high as any odd number. 
The remove curse spell can still be used even without 
ingredients, but the character has disadvantage on the rolls 
against the hag. 
All items used for cursing or removing a curse disappear 
when used.
Cursed Attraction:
The target now attracts insects that bite all over their 
body. Rashes appear and they are unable to sit still due 
to the need to fidget and scratch in various places. 
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. Poison ivy that grew underneath the 
manure of a catoblepas. A jar full of live mosquitos.
Cure. Insect repellent salve created from the leaf and 
root of the marsh cress tree found in tropical locations 
and enchanted with the resistance cantrip.
Cursed Reflection:
The target’s reflection is changed into a grotesque dead 
husk of themself. Others that see this reflection are 
horrified and disgusted.
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. A mirror that has been smashed after 
a banshee has looked into it. The facial skin of a 
dead body.
Cure. You must take the skin of a naga, drape it 
across the cursed, and recite the incantation found on 
the scroll of rejuvenation.
Disrespectful Tongue:
No matter the target’s intentions, everything that 
comes out of their mouth is heard as sarcastic and 
disrespectful.
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. Tongue of a spellcaster who has cast 
vicious mockery. 
Cure. The spittle or bottled breath of a spellcaster 
who has healed a creature.
Harming Blow:
When the target attacks with a weapon and misses, 
they hit themself, dealing half the weapon damage. 
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. One bludgeoning, slashing, or piercing 
weapon that has spilled the blood of the owner's allies. 
Cure. One bludgeoning, slashing, or piercing 
weapon that has spilled the blood of the owner's 
enemies.
Therianthropy:
Therianthropy is typically a condition (lycanthropy 
being the most common type) that is contracted after 
an attack from a werefolk. There are no immediate 
effects from the condition until the next full moon, 
under which the person transforms into the same type 
of werefolk as the one that infected them.
Therianthropy can also be a curse placed on an 
individual by a powerful magical practitioner by 
drawing on the primal magic of the land and dark 
gods of beasts. It can also be inherited. If two werefolk 
have children, there is a chance the child inherits the 
therianthropy.
Turned:
The target is now a target for the Turn Undead ability. 
Friendly spellcasters with this feature cannot exempt 
the target.
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. Desecrated holy symbol. Three fingers 
from a body buried in hallowed ground. 
Cure. Holy water and a symbol blessed by the 
champion of a god.
Unlucky Sea Voyager:
Any boat the target gets on is blown off course and 
shipwrecked far away from its intended destination.
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. Piece of a sail from a shipwreck. 
Cure. You must bring sunken treasure with a value 
score of 7 to the underwater altar of a sea god as an 
offering.
Vampirism:
Vampirism is typically a magical disease that is 
contracted from the bite of a vampire. It takes three 
days for the disease to run its course, culminating in 
the death of the victim. Their corpse is then magically 
reanimated. The vampire or vampire spawn still 
closely resembles the person they were in life with the 
difference being slightly paler skin and fangs where 
their canine teeth were. 
Vampirism can also be a curse placed on an 
individual by a powerful spellcaster. This type of 
vampirism requires text from the Codex Necrotis, a 
powerful book of necromancy.
Vanishing Coin:
The target must spend all the money they receive the 
same day they receive or it disappears. 
Ingredients. One of the target’s personal 
belongings. Coin soaked in the blood of a poor 
person. 
Cure. Coin soaked in the blood of a rich person.
Cures:
The greater restoration spell can remove the condition 
if cast before the new werefolk’s first full moon. The 
remove curse spell can be used either before or after 
the first full moon but requires the hide of a werefolk 
that has the same type of therianthropy as you. The 
wish spell can return the victim to their previous form. 
The greater restoration and remove curse spells do not 
work on werefolk that inherited their therianthropy 
from their parents. Spells that create bodies, such as 
reincarnation, do not remove the therianthropy.
Vampire Spawn:
In Those Who Wander, when you are bitten by a 
vampire you become a vampire spawn, a creature that 
hungers for blood and is under the control of the 
vampire that turned them. The only way to become a 
true vampire is to drink the blood of the vampire that 
turned you. If the vampire is destroyed before turning 
you, you regain your free will.
If you want to follow that lore, the character 
that has been turned gets the following benefits 
and detriments. They are not able to gain further 
detriments or enhancements until they become a full-
fledged vampire. 
You and your storyteller can determine whether 
your character is a special case and have a vampire 
bite be the only requirement to become a vampire. In 
that case, you’ll ignore the vampire spawn effects listed 
below. 
Bat Form.  You can use your action to polymorph 
into a bat, or back into your true form. Any 
equipment you are wearing or carrying isn’t 
transformed. You revert to your true form if you die.
Bite and Claws. As a vampire, your nails and teeth 
are natural weapons. You can take an action to deliver 
a bite attack (damage equal to 1d6 + Strength) or a 
claw attack (1d4 + Strength).
Bloodlust. The first time piercing or slashing 
damage is inflicted on a living creature in combat, you 
must roll a DS 16 Wisdom saving check or go wild 
on your next turn, attacking a random living creature 
within range of your overland speed.
Blood Feeding. Every three days, you must drink 
16 drops of health in blood from a person to keep 
yourself satisfied and at full strength. When you go 
more than three days without feeding, you must roll a

Automatic Effects:
When you shapeshift for the first time under the full 
moon, you automatically gain the following effects:
Bloodlust. The first time piercing or slashing 
damage is inflicted on a living creature in combat, you 
must roll a DS 14 Wisdom saving check or go wild 
on your next turn, attacking a random living creature 
within range of your overland speed.
Hybrid and Beast Form. You can use your action to 
polymorph into a beast-person hybrid or into a beast, 
or back into your true form. Any equipment you are 
wearing or carrying isn’t transformed. You revert to 
your true form if you die.
Lunar Eclipse. You lose all abilities associated with 
your therianthropy the day before, during, and after a 
lunar eclipse.
Regeneration. You replenish 2 drops of health at 
the start of each turn.
Slowed Regeneration. When you suffer damage 
from silver weapons or ammunition, your ability to 
regenerate is negated for 1 round. Your regeneration 
is also negated for 1 round if you suffer fire damage 
and you have the Fire Vulnerability detriment or are 
bitten by a vampire and you have the Vampire Bite 
Vulnerability detriment.
Uncontrolled Shifting. You are forced to shapeshift 
into your hybrid form on the night before the full 
moon, the night of the full moon, and the night after 
the full moon and are not in control of yourself. You 
do not remember what you’ve done on those nights.

Smithing:
(Prerequisite: proficiency with smith’s tools and 
Strength or Agility of +1 or higher)
Smithing allows you to use an anvil to create a variety 
of items from metal bars. Strength is needed for the 
majority of items, while Agility is used for more 
intricate or smaller items. Each item has requirements 
for the number of bars needed to make it.
Requirements:
Enchanting an item requires three things: the 
mundane item one wishes to be enchanted, someone 
to enchant it, and the necessary reagents for the 
enchantment (see the “Reagents” section). The 
mundane item, reagents, and service of an enchanter 
can all be purchased, but an efficient adventurer (or 
one low on wealth) can gather any of the physical 
components or perform the enchantment on 
their own. 
A mundane item can be crafted from raw materials 
(see the “Crafting” section). The reagents can be 
uncovered, bartered for, or gathered from creatures 
throughout the planes. An adventurer with proficiency 
in the Arcana skill or with the Spellcasting feature 
can enchant items. Adventurers with proficiency in 
the Arcana skill must research enchantments but 
retain the ability to imbue researched enchantments. 
A character with the Spellcasting feature can innately 
create enchantments that correlate to a spell they 
know. (An enchantment’s correlated spells are listed in 
its entry in the “Enchantments” section.)
While an adventurer might find it easier to rely on 
their knowledge of spells for enchantments, they don’t 
retain the ability to imbue an enchantment if they 
forget the correlated spell. If a spellcaster wants to 
create an enchantment they don’t know the correlating 
spell of, they must research the enchantment the same 
way an adventurer with proficiency in the Arcana spell 
does. The time necessary to research enchantments of 
certain rarities is listed in the Arcane Research table.
Hours spent researching need not be consecutive, 
but the full amount of time must be spent before the 
enchantment is considered researched. The equivalent 
number of days has been provided. A full day (24 
hours) can be counted off the total time researched if a 
day is dedicated to study and no other activity, even if 
a long rest is taken.

Diseases:
A plague ravages the kingdom, setting the adventurers 
on a quest to find a cure. An adventurer emerges from 
an ancient tomb, unopened for centuries, and soon 
finds herself suffering from a wasting illness. A witch 
offends some dark power and contracts a strange 
affliction that spreads whenever she casts spells.
A simple outbreak might amount to little more than 
a small drain on party resources, curable by a casting 
of lesser restoration. A more complicated outbreak can 
form the basis of one or more adventures as characters 
search for a cure, stop the spread of the disease, and 
deal with the consequences.
A disease that does more than infect a few party 
members is primarily a plot device. The rules help 
describe the effects of the disease and how it can be 
cured, but the specifics of how a disease works aren’t 
bound by a common set of rules. Diseases can affect 
any creature, and a given illness might or might not 
pass from one kind of creature to another. A plague 
might affect only constructs or undead, or sweep 
through those of halfling parentage but leave other 
peoples untouched. What matters is the story you 
want to tell.
Sample Diseases:
The diseases here illustrate the variety of ways disease 
can work in the game. Feel free to alter the saving 
check Difficulty Scores, incubation times, symptoms, 
and other characteristics of these diseases to suit your 
campaign.
Cackle Fever:
This disease targets any person, except those of 
gnomish parentage, who are strangely immune. While 
in the grips of this disease, victims frequently succumb 
to fits of wild laughter, giving the disease its common 
name and its chilling nickname: “the shrieks.”
Symptoms manifest 1d4 hours after infection and 
include fever and disorientation. The infected creature 
suffers one level of exhaustion that can’t be removed 
until the disease is cured.
Any event that causes the infected creature great 
stress—including entering combat, suffering damage, 
experiencing fear, or having a nightmare—forces the 
creature to make a DS 13 Health saving check. On 
a failed check, the creature suffers 5 (1d10) psychic 
damage and becomes incapacitated with laughter for 
1 minute. The creature can repeat the saving check at 
the end of each of its turns, ending the laughter and 
the incapacitated condition on a success.
Any person who starts their turn within 10 feet of 
an infected creature in the throes of laughter must 
succeed on a DS 10 Health saving check or also 
become infected with the disease. Once a creature 
succeeds on this check, it is immune to the wild 
laughter of that particular infected creature for 
24 hours.
At the end of each long rest, an infected creature 
can make a DS 13 Health saving check. On a 
successful check, the DS for this check and for the 
check to avoid an attack of wild laughter drops by 
1d6. When the saving check DS drops to 0, the 
creature recovers from the disease. A creature that 
fails three of these saving checks falls unconscious and 
must begin making death rolls.
Sewer Plague:
Sewer plague is a generic term for a broad category 
of illnesses that incubate in sewers, refuse heaps, 
and stagnant swamps, and which are sometimes 
transmitted by creatures that dwell in those areas, such 
as rats and otyughs.
When a person is bitten by a creature that carries 
the disease, or when they come into contact with filth 
or offal contaminated by the disease, the person must 
succeed on a DS 11 Health saving check or become 
infected.
It takes 1d4 days for sewer plague’s symptoms to 
manifest in an infected person. Symptoms include 
fatigue and cramps. The infected person suffers one 
level of exhaustion, and they regain only half the 
normal number of drops of health from spending 
Health Dice and no drops of health from finishing 
a long rest. At the end of each long rest, an infected 
creature must make a DS 11 Health saving check. 
On a failed check, the character suffers one level of 
exhaustion. On a successful check, the character’s
Sight Rot:
This painful infection causes bleeding from the eyes 
and eventually blinds a sighted creature.
A person or beast that drinks water tainted by sight 
rot must succeed on a DS 15 Health saving check or 
become infected. One day after infection, a sighted 
creature’s vision starts to become blurry. The creature 
suffers a −1 penalty to attack checks and ability checks 
that rely on sight. At the end of each long rest after 
the symptoms appear, the penalty worsens by 1. When 
it reaches −5, the creature is disoriented until its sight 
is restored by magic, such as lesser restoration or heal. 
After six months of blindness, the person or beast 
removes the disoriented condition and makes one of 
its senses other than sighted, if any, its primary sense.
Crime:
Sometimes crime pays. Over the course of an 
adventure, characters might want to engage in certain 
illicit activities to turn a profit. Below are examples of 
crimes a character could engage in.
Heist. Characters can case a location, figure out 
entry points, and make a plan to rob the place of all 
its riches. This is a medium-level crime. Those caught 
are going to be forced to return the items, pay a fine, 
and spend at least a week in prison.
Pickpocketing. Quick-and-easy characters can move 
through a crowd and silently relieve those around 
them of their earnings and other valuable items. This 
is a low-level crime and the response, if caught, is 
minimal, usually a fine, being forced to return the 
items, and sometimes spending a few days in prison.
Ransoming. Characters who are brave enough to 
kidnap an individual can try and ransom them for 
money. This, along with robbery where a person’s life 
is being threatened, is one of the more dangerous 
crimes a character can commit. This is a high-level 
crime that can easily land characters in jail for years, if 
not swift execution, depending on who the target is. 
Robbery. Similar to a heist, this has an extra level 
of danger due to the violence involved. Oftentimes 
individuals’ lives are deliberately put in danger in 
order to get the goods quicker and easier. If characters 
choose to go the route of threatening others and are 
successful at doing so, the DS lowers by 2.
Crime Tables:
Chances of Finding a Target. Depending on what 
type of crime characters want to engage in, there’s a 
chance that crime can’t be done in the settlement they 
are currently in. Tables that include chances of finding 
a target are there to help the storyteller determine 
whether or not a target exists. 
DS to Find Target. Characters interested in 
executing a crime must first find a target. The 
smaller the settlement is, the harder it is to find a 
suitable one, due to funds, location, and any other 
number of factors. Interested characters must make 
an Intelligence (Investigation) check matching or 
exceeding the DS to find a target.
DS to Investigate. Depending on the crime, once 
a target has been found, it has to be investigated. 
The storyteller can decide how many checks must be 
made to fully investigate the target, but the average 
of the checks must equal or exceed the DS. Any other 
necessary checks use the same DS.
DS to Succeed. Depending on the target chosen, 
there might need to be a number of checks made. 
Agility (Stealth) checks to enter the place undetected, 
Intelligence (Investigation) checks to search for 
anything, Agility (Legerdemain) checks to steal items, 
and other Agility checks using thieves’ tools to bypass 
locks. How many and what kind of checks needed are 
up to the storyteller, but the average of the rolls must 
equal or exceed the DS for the heist to succeed.
Payout. Once you have successfully executed a 
crime, you’re either left with coins in your hands or 
items that need to be sold. For items, you need to find 
someone willing to buy potentially stolen goods, such 
as a fence. 
Each phase of a crime, at minimum, takes one 
hour. The storyteller can decide if it takes longer. 
In that event, the stages of the crime that are about 
gathering information can be done at different one-
hour intervals, but the actual crimes must be done all 
at once. Payout is not included in the listed time.
Gambling:
Games of chance can be a quick and easy way to make 
a fortune...but they can also be a great way to lose 
everything. 
DS to Find. Depending on the location, finding 
somewhere to gamble can be hard. Smaller settlements 
are less likely to have dedicated places or even people 
gambling out in the open for the characters to find. 
Maximum Bet. Depending on the size of a 
settlement, the amount of money the denizens have 
to spend gambling while still making a living varies 
greatly. A thorp might only be able to afford to 
pay out bets equivalent to a value score of 1 while 
a metropolis can afford high rollers throwing the 
equivalent of a value score of 9.
DS to Win. As the storyteller, you can either require 
only one roll or multiple rolls when it comes to the 
character gambling. Either way, the single roll or the 
average number of the multiple roll must equal the 
DS. Depending on what is rolled, the results may vary.
Result. Depending on what the character rolls 
during the actual gambling phase, there are a number 
of outcomes:
Passing the DS by 5. You win double what you bet. 
So if you bet the equivalent of a value score of 1 and 
you beat the DS by 5, you get your bet back plus the 
equivalent of a value score of 2.
Success. Your bet is matched. So if you bet the 
equivalent of a value score of 1, you get your bet back 
and an additional 1, at minimum.
Failure. You lose your bet.
Failing the DS by 5. You lose double your bet. So 
if you bet the equivalent of a value score of 1 and 
you fail the DS by 5, you lose your bet and owe the 
equivalent of a value score of 2.

through mechanical means are known as tinkerers. 
They are masters of innovation, creating the smallest 
of toys to the largest of constructs. Their mechanical 
prowess is unrivaled by most and their inventions awe 
and wonder those around them.
Creating Schematics. In order to build something, 
you need schematics for it. Typically, schematics are 
bought. Depending on your world, they can be widely 
available or very rare. In other instances, tinkerers 
create their own schematics when they have original 
ideas. Creating schematics replaces the need to 
research them. 
Researching Schematics. For schematics a tinkerer 
hasn’t created, you need to spend a number of 
hours researching them before you are able to build. 
Additional hours of study give a bonus when the item 
is created.
Obtaining Ingredients. The ingredients for making 
items come in their raw form, such as metal bars, or 
their final form: cogs, screws, gears, and more. The 
finalized items can be bought, or they can be created 
through blacksmithing. 
Crafting Items. Once the schematics have been 
studied and all the necessary material has been 
gathered, you can start crafting the items. Smaller 
items, such as the clockwork toy, fire starter, or music 
box, can be made without the need of a workshop. For 
all other items, a workshop is necessary.
Enchanting:
Secluded within an arcane sanctum, an infernal elf 
lifts up the product of his labor: a pendant gleaming 
with radiant energy. After hours of dedicated effort, an 
orc tailor painstakingly stitches the last details into an 
ornate court gown for her upcoming mission.
Where a well-crafted set of armor doesn’t suffice, 
one enchanted with extra defenses or to resist a certain 
kind of magic just might. Enchanting is the practice 
of granting magical properties to otherwise mundane 
items. The task is carried out by a person well-versed 
in arcane studies or spellcasting using rare and magical 
reagents found throughout the planes. 
Compared to inherently magical items, enchanted 
items are typically weaker, but are easier to find and 
create. In fact, enchanting items is a studied skill 
that is comparable to spellcasting, and with the right 
supplies and dedicated time, a passionate arcane 
researcher or knowledgable spellcaster can enchant 
their own items. For everyone else, there are plenty 
of people who make a livelihood enchanting, and 
a sizable community is bound to have at least one 
enchanter.
Rules and Restrictions:
There are several rules and restrictions involved with 
enchanting items:
•	 A magic item that requires attunement cannot be 
enchanted.
•	 An item can only be affected by a maximum of 2 
enchantments.
•	 Several enchantments are considered exclusive. A 
character can only gain the benefit of an exclusive 
enchantment once. If a character attempts to wield 
or use two different items with the same exclusive 
enchantment, they only gain its benefits once.
•	 An enchanted item is considered a mundane item 
affected by magic. If the detect magic spell is cast 
on an enchanted item, the caster becomes aware 
of the enchantment but realizes it’s not intrinsic
Reagents:
An enchantment’s strength and properties are derived 
from the reagents they are created with. These rare 
and powerful materials are gathered from a myriad of 
magical creatures across the planes. However, reagents 
don’t have to be acquired with violence. When 
avoiding conflict, adventurers may instead barter for 
reagents or earn them through quests taken on behalf 
of the creatures. In addition, reagents don’t have to be 
fresh, so they can be discovered in caches of treasure 
or taken from abandoned arcane sanctums. 
The challenge score of a creature determines the 
rarity and value score of the reagent, as listed in 
the Reagent Rarities table, while the creature’s type 
determines which properties it grants an enchantment, 
as listed in the Reagent Properties table. At the 
storyteller’s discretion, greater restrictions can be 
imposed on the specific reagents required for an 
enchantment. For example, an enchantment that 
protects against the petrified condition might require a 
cockatrice gizzard specifically, rather than just a fabled 
material. The Reagent Properties table gives some 
examples of creatures and the specific reagents they 
could provide, but storytellers are encouraged to flavor 
reagents in ways that make sense for their setting 
and story.
If reagents are taken from creatures after combat, 
a storyteller can choose to have characters gather the 
reagents automatically, over a period of time, or by 
making either an Intelligence (Arcana) or Wisdom 
(Environment) check. The Gathering table provides 
guidance for the skill check DS and gathering times.
Enchanting an Item:
Once all the necessities for enchantment are prepared, 
a character is ready for their mundane item to be 
enchanted. The Enchantments table lists, by rarity, 
the time it takes to have an item enchanted, the 
enchantment’s Difficulty Score, the value score 
of having the item enchanted by a professional 
enchanter, and the total value score of buying the 
reagents alongside an enchanter’s services. 
Enchanting an item requires continuous work 
for the listed number of hours. If the enchanter is 
interrupted for any reason, roll a d20. On a 1, the 
reagents are ruined irrevocably and cannot be used 
to perform the enchantment again. If a character 
is performing the enchantment, they must succeed 
on a skill check against the enchantment DS using 
their spellcasting ability bonus (if enchanting using 
a correlating spell) or their Intelligence (Arcana), if 
enchanting using a researched enchantment. On a 
failed check, the enchantment time is doubled. If the 
character fails the check by 5 or more, roll a d20. On 
a 1, the character successfully enchants the item, but 
the item gains a random enchantment of equal rarity.
Exploration:
Worldbuilding can be a difficult task, especially when 
characters unexpectedly choose to go off into the 
unknown. This system is always ready to provide the 
next piece of the map.
Simply identify a location in the bulleted list below 
that approximates the last known place the characters 
visited, then read the description of the area. You 
are provided with both adventure seeds to get your 
creativity going and possible nearby locations to 
choose from to fill in blank spots on the map.
Using this exploration system can be a storyteller 
activity between play sessions, a failsafe mid-session 
when characters do something unexpected, or a group 
activity the players and storyteller can do  together.
The tables provided are suggestions, with adventure 
hooks and nearby locations selected randomly by 
rolling dice, or they can be treated as short lists of 
options to choose from as you see fit.
You can create an entire fantasy campaign setting 
using this system, building out the world piece by 
piece. Or just use it as a storytelling aid, as needed.

Factions can be an important part of any setting. They 
can give players more avenues for quests, obtaining 
knowledge, and fleshing out who their character is. 
This system fleshes out the existing faction system 
by listing the different benefits each rank gets and 
providing a number of quests for each faction.

or lost. Each faction has its own goals and ideals, and

Objects:
When characters need to saw through ropes, shatter 
a window, or smash a vampire’s coffin, the only hard 
and fast rule is this: given enough time and the right 
tools, characters can destroy any destructible object. 
Use common sense when determining a character’s 
success at damaging an object. Can a fighter cut 
through a section of a stone wall with a sword? No, 
the sword is likely to break before the wall does.
For the purpose of these rules, an object is a 
discrete, inanimate item like a window, door, sword, 
book, table, chair, or stone, not a building or a vehicle 
that is composed of many other objects.
Statistics for Objects
When time is a factor, you can assign a defense score 
and health pool depth to a destructible object. You can 
also give it immunities, resistances, and vulnerabilities 
to specific types of damage.
Defense Score. An object’s defense score is a 
measure of how difficult it is to inflict damage to 
the object when striking it (because the object has 
no chance of dodging out of the way). The Object 
Defense Score table provides suggested defense scores 
for various substances.

Traps:
Traps can be found almost anywhere. One wrong 
step in an ancient tomb might trigger a series of 
scything blades, which cleave through armor and 
bone. The seemingly innocuous vines that hang over 
a cave entrance might grasp and choke anyone who 
pushes through them. A net hidden among the trees 
might drop on travelers who pass underneath. In a 
fantasy game, unwary adventurers can fall to their 
deaths, be burned alive, or fall under a fusillade of 
poisoned darts.
A trap can be either mechanical or magical in 
nature. Mechanical traps include pits, arrow traps, 
falling blocks, water-filled rooms, whirling blades, 
and anything else that depends on a mechanism to 
operate. Magic traps are either magical device traps 
or spell traps. Magical device traps initiate spell effects 
when activated. Spell traps are spells such as glyph of 
warding and symbol that function as traps.
Traps in Play:
When adventurers come across a trap, you need to 
know how the trap is triggered and what it does, as 
well as the possibility for the characters to detect the 
trap and to disable or avoid it.
Triggering a Trap:
Most traps are triggered when a creature goes 
somewhere or touches something that the trap’s 
creator wanted to protect. Common triggers include 
stepping on a pressure plate or a false section of floor, 
pulling a trip wire, turning a doorknob, and using the 
wrong key in a lock. Magic traps are often set to go off 
when a creature enters an area or touches an object. 
Some magic traps (such as the glyph of warding spell) 
have more complicated trigger conditions, including a 
password that prevents the trap from activating.
Detecting and 
Disabling a Trap
Usually, some element of a trap is visible to careful 
inspection. Characters might notice an uneven 
flagstone that conceals a pressure plate, spot the gleam 
of light off a tripwire, notice small holes in the walls 
from which jets of flame will erupt, or otherwise 
detect something that points to a trap’s presence.
A trap’s description specifies the checks and 
Difficulty Scores needed to detect it, disable it, or 
both. A character actively looking for a trap can 
attempt a Wisdom (Perception) check against the 
trap’s DS. You can also compare the DS to detect 
the trap with each character’s Wisdom (Perception) 
skill score to determine whether anyone in the party 
notices the trap in passing. If the adventurers detect a 
trap before triggering it, they might be able to disarm 
it, either permanently or long enough to move past 
it. You might call for an Intelligence (Investigation) 
check for a character to deduce what needs to be done, 
followed by an Agility check using thieves’ tools to 
perform the necessary sabotage.
Any character can attempt an Intelligence (Arcana) 
check to detect or disarm a magic trap, in addition 
to any other checks noted in the trap’s description. 
The Difficulty Scores are the same regardless of the 
check used. In addition, dispel magic has a chance of 
disabling most magic traps. A magic trap’s description 
provides the DS for the ability check made when you 
use dispel magic.
In most cases, a trap’s description is clear enough 
that you can adjudicate whether a character’s actions 
locate or foil the trap. As with many situations, you
Trap Effects:
The effects of traps can range from inconvenient to 
deadly, making use of elements such as arrows, spikes, 
blades, poison, toxic gas, blasts of fire, and deep pits. 
The deadliest traps combine multiple elements to kill, 
injure, contain, or drive off any creature unfortunate 
enough to trigger them. A trap’s description specifies 
what happens when it is triggered.
The attack of a trap, the save DS to resist its effects, 
and the damage it inflicts can vary depending on the 
trap’s severity. Use the Trap Save and Attack DS table 
and the Damage Severity by Step table for suggestions 
based on three levels of trap severity.
A trap intended to be a setback is unlikely to kill 
or seriously harm characters of the indicated levels, 
whereas a dangerous trap is likely to seriously injure 
(and potentially kill) characters of the indicated 
levels. A deadly trap is likely to kill characters of the 
indicated steps.

Complex Traps:
Complex traps work like standard traps, except once 
activated they execute a series of actions each round. A 
complex trap turns the process of dealing with a trap 
into something more like a combat encounter.
When a complex trap activates, determine combat 
order—initiative order if the adventurers sprang the 
trap unawares, lookout order if they spotted it, sleuth 
order if they deduced it was there by picking up clues. 
The trap’s description includes combat order bonuses. 
On its turn, the trap activates again, often taking 
an action. It might make successive attacks against 
intruders, create an effect that changes over time, or 
otherwise produce a dynamic challenge. Otherwise, 
the complex trap can be detected and disabled or 
bypassed in the usual ways.
For example, a trap that causes a room to slowly 
flood works best as a complex trap. On the trap’s turn, 
the water level rises. After several rounds, the room is 
completely flooded.
Sample Traps:
The magical and mechanical traps presented here vary 
in deadliness and are presented in alphabetical order.
Collapsing Roof:
Mechanical trap
This trap uses a trip wire to collapse the supports 
keeping an unstable section of a ceiling in place.
The trip wire is 3 inches off the ground and 
stretches between two support beams. The DS to spot 
the trip wire is 10. A successful DS 15 Agility check 
using thieves’ tools disables the trip wire harmlessly. A 
character without thieves’ tools can attempt this check
Fire-Breathing Statue:
Magic trap
This trap is activated when an intruder steps on a 
hidden pressure plate, releasing a magical gout of 
flame from a nearby statue. The statue can be of 
anything, including a dragon or a wizard casting 
a spell.
The DS is 15 to spot the pressure plate, as well as 
faint scorch marks on the floor and walls. A spell or 
other effect that can sense the presence of magic, such 
as detect magic, reveals an aura of evocation magic 
around the statue.
The trap activates when more than 20 pounds of 
weight is placed on the pressure plate, causing the 
statue to release a 30-foot cone of fire. Each creature 
in the fire must make a DS 13 Agility saving check, 
suffering 22 (4d10) fire damage on a failed check, or 
half as much damage on a successful one.
Wedging an iron spike or other object under the 
pressure plate prevents the trap from activating. A 
successful dispel magic (DS 13) cast on the statue 
destroys the trap.
Pits:
Mechanical trap
Four basic pit traps are presented here.
Simple Pit. A simple pit trap is a hole dug in the 
ground. The hole is covered by a large cloth anchored 
on the pit’s edge and camouflaged with dirt and 
debris.
The DS to spot the pit is 10. Anyone stepping 
on the cloth falls through and pulls the cloth down 
into the pit, taking damage based on the pit’s depth 
(usually 10 feet, but some pits are deeper).
Hidden Pit. This pit has a cover constructed from 
material identical to the floor around it.
A successful DS 15 Wisdom (Perception) check 
discerns an absence of foot traffic over the section 
of floor that forms the pit’s cover. A successful DS 
15 Intelligence (Investigation) check is necessary to 
confirm that the trapped section of floor is actually the 
cover of a pit.
When a creature steps on the cover, it swings open 
like a trapdoor, causing the intruder to spill into the 
pit below. The pit is usually 10 or 20 feet deep but can 
be deeper.
Once the pit trap is detected, an iron spike or 
similar object can be wedged between the pit’s cover 
and the surrounding floor in such a way as to prevent 
the cover from opening, thereby making it safe to 
cross. The cover can also be magically held shut using 
the arcane lock spell or similar magic.
Locking Pit. This pit trap is identical to a hidden pit 
trap, with one key exception: the trap door that covers 
the pit is spring-loaded. After a creature falls into the 
pit, the cover snaps shut to trap its victim inside.
A successful DS 20 Strength check is necessary to 
pry the cover open. The cover can also be smashed 
open. A character in the pit can also attempt to disable 
the spring mechanism from the inside with a DS 15 
Agility check using thieves’ tools, provided that the 
mechanism can be reached and the character can see
Poison Darts:
Mechanical trap
When a creature steps on a hidden pressure plate, 
poison-tipped darts shoot from spring-loaded 
or pressurized tubes cleverly embedded in the 
surrounding walls. An area might include multiple 
pressure plates, each one rigged to its own set of darts.
The tiny holes in the walls are obscured by dust 
and cobwebs, or cleverly hidden amid bas-reliefs, 
murals, or frescoes that adorn the walls. The DS to 
spot them is 15. With a successful DS 15 Intelligence 
(Investigation) check, a character can deduce the 
presence of the pressure plate from variations in the 
mortar and stone used to create it, compared to the 
surrounding floor. Wedging an iron spike or other 
object under the pressure plate prevents the trap 
from activating. Stuffing the holes with cloth or wax 
prevents the darts contained within from launching.
The trap activates when more than 20 pounds 
of weight is placed on the pressure plate, releasing 
four darts. Each dart makes a ranged attack (DS 14) 
against a random target within 10 feet of the pressure 
plate (vision is irrelevant to this attack roll). (If there 
are no targets in the area, the darts don’t hit anything.) 
A target that is hit suffers 2 (1d4) piercing damage 
and must succeed on a DS 15 Health saving check, 
suffering 11 (2d10) poison damage on a failed check, 
or half as much damage on a successful one.
Poison Needle:
Mechanical trap
A poisoned needle is hidden within a treasure chest’s 
lock, or in something else that a creature might open. 
Opening the chest without the proper key causes the 
needle to spring out, delivering a dose of poison.
When the trap is triggered, the needle extends 3 
inches straight out from the lock. A creature within 
range suffers 1 piercing damage and 11 (2d10) poison 
damage, and must succeed on a DS 15 Health saving 
check or be sickened for 1 hour.
A successful DS 20 Intelligence (Investigation) 
check allows a character to deduce the trap’s presence 
from alterations made to the lock to accommodate the 
needle. A successful DS 15 Agility check using thieves’ 
tools disarms the trap, removing the needle from 
the lock. Unsuccessfully attempting to pick the lock 
triggers the trap.
Rolling Sphere:
Mechanical trap
When 20 or more pounds of pressure are placed on 
this trap’s pressure plate, a hidden trapdoor in the 
ceiling opens, releasing a 10-foot-diameter rolling 
sphere of solid stone.
With a successful DS 15 Wisdom (Perception) 
check, a character can spot the trapdoor and pressure 
plate. A search of the floor accompanied by a 
successful DS 15 Intelligence (Investigation) check 
reveals variations in the mortar and stone that betray 
the pressure plate’s presence. The same check made 
while inspecting the ceiling notes variations in the 
stonework that reveal the trapdoor. Wedging an iron 
spike or other object under the pressure plate prevents 
the trap from activating.
Activation of the sphere requires all creatures to take 
turns in combat order. The sphere has the equivalent 
of an Agility of +8, an Intelligence of +0, and a 
Wisdom of +8 for the purposes of combat order. On 
its turn, it moves 60 feet in a straight line. The sphere 
can move through creatures’ spaces, and creatures 
can move through its space, treating it as difficult 
terrain. Whenever the sphere enters a creature’s space 
or a creature enters its space while it’s rolling, that 
creature must succeed on a DS 15 Agility saving check 
or suffer 55 (10d10) bludgeoning damage and be 
knocked prone.
The sphere stops when it hits a wall or similar 
barrier. It can’t go around corners, but smart builders 
incorporate gentle, curving turns into nearby passages 
that allow the sphere to keep moving.
As an action, a creature within 5 feet of the sphere 
can attempt to slow it down with a DS 20 Strength 
check. On a successful check, the sphere’s speed is 
reduced by 15 feet. If the sphere’s speed drops to 0, it 
stops moving and is no longer a threat.
